The statement for \V is the same argument applied to \A\T=\V D U\T. The four Penrose conditions for \V D^{-1} U\T follow from  U\T U=\V\T\V=\I_r. For instance, \A\A^+= U U\T and \A^+\A=\V\V\T are symmetric. Completing  U and \V to orthogonal matrices gives the full SVD \A=	ilde{ U}	ilde{ D}	ilde{\V}\T, with 	ilde{ D} of size m	imes n carrying \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. By convention, \sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{\min(m,n)}=0. Geometrically, \A maps the unit ball of \Real^n onto a solid ellipsoid in \C(\A) with semi-axes \sigma_i u_i. The input direction  v_i is stretched by the factor \sigma_i and turned into  u_i. The Moore–Penrose inverse undoes the stretching on \C(\A) and sends \C(\A)\perpc to zero. The matrix  U U\T is the orthogonal projection onto \C(\A), whose theory is in Chapter 6. [Norms and extremal properties] Let \A be m	imes n with singular values \sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots, and let 
orm{\A}_2=\max_{\x
e zero}
orm{\A\x}/
orm{\x} be the spectral norm. 1. 
orm{\A}_2=\sigma_1 and 
orm{\A}_F^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2. 2. If \A has full column rank n, then \min_{\x
e zero}
orm{\A\x}/
orm{\x}=\sigma_n, attained at  v_n. 3. (Eckart–Young.) For k<r, let \A_k=\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i u_i v_i\T. Then 
orm{\A-\B}_2\ge\sigma_{k+1}=
orm{\A-\A_k}_2 for every \B with ank(\B)\le k. (a) and (b): 
orm{\A\x}^2/
orm{\x}^2=\x\T\A\T\A\x/\x\T\x, and the eigenvalues of \A\T\A are the \sigma_i^2 (padded with zeros), so @thm-mat-extremal-rayleigh applies. For the Frobenius norm, 
orm{\A}_F^2=	r(\A\T\A)=\sum\sigma_i^2 by @prp-mat-eigen-basic(a). (b) \A-\A_k=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i u_i v_i\T has largest singular value \sigma_{k+1}. If ank(\B)\le k, then \dim\Null(\B)\ge n-k, and since (n-k)+(k+1)>n, a basis of \Null(\B) together with  v_1,\dots, v_{k+1} is dependent. So the two subspaces share a unit vector \x=\sum_{i\le k+1}c_i v_i. Then 
orm{(\A-\B)\x}^2=
orm{\A\x}^2=\sum_{i\le k+1}\sigma_i^2c_i^2\ge\sigma_{k+1}^2. The Frobenius version of (c), 
orm{\A-\B}_F^2\ge\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2, also holds (Eckart and Young 1936). It is the basis of principal components. The condition number [Condition number] The condition number of an m	imes n matrix \A of full column rank is \kappa(\A)= rac{\sigma_{\max}(\A)}{\sigma_{\min}(\A)}= rac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_n}. For a nonsingular square matrix this equals 
orm{\A}_2
orm{\A^{-1}}_2. A matrix without full column rank has \kappa(\A)=\infty by convention. By @prp-mat-svd-norms, \kappa(\A) is the ratio of the largest to the smallest stretching that \A applies to a unit vector. It is at least 1, is unchanged by scaling \A or multiplying it on the left by a matrix with orthonormal columns, and equals 1 iff \A\T\A=c\I, that is, iff the columns are orthogonal with equal lengths. Two further facts explain its role in regression. First, the singular values of \A\T\A are the \sigma_i^2, so \kappa(\A\T\A)=\kappa(\A)^2 . {#eq-mat-kappa-squared} Second, \kappa bounds how much relative errors in the data can grow when a linear system is solved. If \A is square and nonsingular, \A\x= b and \A(\x+\delta\x)= b+\delta b, then \delta\x=\A^{-1}\delta b, and 
orm{ b}\le\sigma_1
orm{\x} gives  rac{
orm{\delta\x}}{
orm{\x}}\le rac{
orm{\A^{-1}}_2
orm{\delta b}}{
orm{ b}/\sigma_1} =\kappa(\A)\, rac{
orm{\delta b}}{
orm{ b}} . {#eq-mat-perturbation} In floating point, relative errors of about 10^{-16} in the data can therefore become errors of about \kappa	imes10^{-16} in the solution. Solving the normal equations works with \X\T\X and so, by @eq-mat-kappa-squared, squares the damage. Chapter 6 and Chapter 10 take this up. A small \sigma_{\min} has a direct statistical reading. By @prp-mat-svd-norms(b), 
orm{\X v_n}=\sigma_n with 
orm{ v_n}=1. The coefficients  v_n combine the columns of \X into a vector that is nearly zero, which is a near-dependence among the regressors. This is the basis of the collinearity diagnostics of Chapter 26. The size of \kappa depends on the units of the columns, so columns are usually rescaled before it is interpreted. [A macroeconomic design] Take the 203 quarterly US observations of real GDP, real investment, real government spending, real disposable income, population and unemployment, with an intercept, as a model matrix with p=7 columns. As recorded, \kappa(\X)=5.10	imes 10^{5}. Most of that is units: GDP is measured in billions and unemployment in percent. Rescaling each column to unit length reduces it to 383, and centring the regressors before rescaling reduces it further to 124. By @eq-mat-kappa-squared the corresponding cross-product matrix has condition number 15386. What remains is not an artefact of units. Figure 1.8.1(b) shows the right singular vector for the smallest singular value, \sigma_{\min}=0.0175, of the centred and scaled design. Its weight is concentrated on GDP (0.78) and disposable income (-0.61). The combination of the scaled columns with these coefficients is a vector of length 0.0175, although every column has length one. The two series move almost in lockstep: their correlation is 0.9990. No rescaling can separate their coefficients well. Centring is not a neutral choice, however: it removes near-dependences that involve the intercept, and Belsley et al. (1980) recommend scaling without centring for that reason, so their diagnostics would use the unit-length figure 383. Chapter 26 returns to the choice. The listing computes the singular values, and the script also checks @eq-mat-kappa-squared, the Penrose conditions for \V D^{-1} U\T, and the Eckart–Young bound. [Figure 1.8.1. Singular value decomposition of a macroeconomic model matrix (@exm-mat-macro-svd). (a) Singular values relative to the largest, for the columns as recorded, rescaled to unit length, and centred then rescaled. The ratio of the first to the last is the condition number. (b) The right singular vector for the smallest singular value of the centred design. Its two large loadings reveal a near-dependence between GDP and disposable income.] Figure 1.8.1. Singular value decomposition of a macroeconomic model matrix (@exm-mat-macro-svd). (a) Singular values relative to the largest, for the columns as recorded, rescaled to unit length, and centred then rescaled. The ratio of the first to the last is the condition number. (b) The right singular vector for the smallest singular value of the centred design. Its two large loadings reveal a near-dependence between GDP and disposable income. [Singular value decomposition of a macroeconomic model matrix (@exm-mat-macro-svd). (a) Singular values relative to the largest, for the columns as recorded, rescaled to unit length, and centred then rescaled. The ratio of the first to the last is the condition number. (b) The right singular vector for the smallest singular value of the centred design. Its two large loadings reveal a near-dependence between GDP and disposable income.] Singular value decomposition of a macroeconomic model matrix (@exm-mat-macro-svd). (a) Singular values relative to the largest, for the columns as recorded, rescaled to unit length, and centred then rescaled. The ratio of the first to the last is the condition number. (b) The right singular vector for the smallest singular value of the centred design. Its two large loadings reveal a near-dependence between GDP and disposable income. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm data = sm.datasets.macrodata.load_pandas().data names = ["realgdp", "realinv", "realgovt", "realdpi", "pop", "unemp"] labels = ["GDP", "investment", "government", "disp. income", "population", "unemployment"] Z = data[names].to_numpy() n = len(Z) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Z]) # as recorded X_unit = X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0) # unit-length columns Xc = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Z - Z.mean(axis=0)]) # regressors centred X_std = Xc / np.linalg.norm(Xc, axis=0) # ... then length 1 for name, M in [("raw", X), ("unit length", X_unit), ("centred", X_std)]: U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M, full_matrices=False) # M = U diag(s) V' print(f"{name:12s} kappa = {s[0] / s[-1]:10.1f} singular values / s_1:", np.array2string(s / s[0], precision=4)) Exercises B. Practice [B1] Let \X=[\x_1,\x_2] with 
orm{\x_1}=
orm{\x_2}=1 and \x_1\T\x_2=r, \lvert rvert<1. Show that \kappa(\X)=\sqrt{(1+\lvert rvert)/(1-\lvert rvert)}. How large must \lvert rvert be for \kappa(\X)>30? \X\T\X= egin{psmallmatrix}1&r\r&1\end{psmallmatrix} has eigenvalues 1\pm r, with eigenvectors (1,\pm1)\T. The singular values of \X are their square roots, so \kappa(\X)^2=(1+\lvert rvert)/(1-\lvert rvert). For \kappa>30 we need (1+\lvert rvert)/(1-\lvert rvert)>900, that is, \lvert rvert>899/901\approx0.998. For two columns, even \kappa(\X)=100 requires \lvert rvert>9999/10001\approx0.9998. [B2] Show that \kappa(\X)\ge\max_j
orm{\x_j}/\min_k
orm{\x_k}, so that columns on very different scales force a large condition number. Show by example that rescaling the columns can also increase \kappa.

title: 1.9 Idempotent matrices
content:
Idempotent matrices A square matrix \A is idempotent if \A^2=\A. Applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once, which is how a projection behaves. Examples are \I,  zero, the centring matrix of @exm-mat-centring, the products \A\G and \G\A for a generalized inverse \G (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(a)), and the non-symmetric  egin{psmallmatrix}1&1\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}. In linear models, sums of squares are quadratic forms in symmetric idempotent matrices, and their degrees of freedom are ranks. [General idempotent matrices] Let \A be n	imes n and idempotent of rank r. 1. Every eigenvalue of \A is 0 or 1. 2. ank(\A)=	r(\A). 3. \I-\A is idempotent, \A(\I-\A)=(\I-\A)\A= zero, \C(\I-\A)=\Null(\A), and ank(\A)+ank(\I-\A)=n. 4. An idempotent matrix that is nonsingular equals \I. 5. \mathbf{P}^{-1}\A\mathbf{P} is idempotent for nonsingular \mathbf{P}, and \A\T is idempotent. (a) If \A\x=\lambda\x with \x
e zero, then \lambda\x=\A\x=\A^2\x=\lambda^2\x, so \lambda^2=\lambda. (b) If r=0 both sides vanish. Otherwise take a rank factorization \A=\B\mathbf{F} (@thm-mat-row-col-rank). Then \B\mathbf{F}\B\mathbf{F}=\B\mathbf{F}. Since \B has full column rank and \mathbf{F} has full row rank, \B has a left inverse and \mathbf{F} a right inverse (Section 1.3), and cancelling them gives \mathbf{F}\B=\I_r. So 	r(\A)=	r(\B\mathbf{F})=	r(\mathbf{F}\B)=r by @thm-mat-trace-cyclic. (c) The first two claims are one-line expansions. \C(\I-\A)\subseteq\Null(\A) because \A(\I-\A)= zero, and  v\in\Null(\A) gives  v=(\I-\A) v. The rank statement is then rank–nullity. (d) Multiply \A^2=\A by \A^{-1}. (e) (\mathbf{P}^{-1}\A\mathbf{P})^2=\mathbf{P}^{-1}\A^2\mathbf{P} and (\A\T)^2=(\A^2)\T. By (c), every \x splits as \A\x+(\I-\A)\x with the first part in \C(\A) and the second in \Null(\A). So \Real^n=\C(\A)\dirsum\Null(\A), and \A projects onto \C(\A) along \Null(\A). The projection is orthogonal exactly when the two subspaces are orthogonal, which happens iff \A is symmetric (@exr-mat-oblique). [Symmetric idempotent matrices] Let \A be an n	imes n symmetric matrix of rank r. Then \A is idempotent iff all its eigenvalues are 0 or 1. In that case 1. \A=\Q_1\Q_1\T, where the n	imes r matrix \Q_1 has orthonormal columns spanning \C(\A); 2. ank(\A)=	r(\A)=r, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 1; 3. \A and \I-\A are nonnegative definite, and \x\T\A\x=
orm{\A\x}^2\le
orm{\x}^2. If \A is idempotent its eigenvalues are 0 or 1 by @prp-mat-idempotent-basic(a). Conversely, if \A=\Q Lambda\Q\T with each \lambda_i\in\{0,1\}, then \A^2=\Q Lambda^2\Q\T=\Q Lambda\Q\T=\A. In that case, order the eigenvalues so that the r ones come first and let \Q_1 hold the corresponding eigenvectors. Then \A=\Q Lambda\Q\T=\Q_1\Q_1\T, and \C(\A)=\C(\Q_1) by @cor-mat-spectral-consequences(a). This is (a). The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues, which is (b). For (c), the eigenvalues of \A and of \I-\A are nonnegative, and \x\T\A\x=\x\T\A\T\A\x. Also 
orm{\x}^2-
orm{\A\x}^2=\x\T(\I-\A)\x\ge0. Chapter 6 shows that symmetric idempotent matrices are exactly the orthogonal projections, and \Q_1\Q_1\T in (a) is the projection onto \C(\A). In Chapter 4, part (b) becomes the degrees of freedom of a chi-squared distribution. [Sums of symmetric idempotent matrices] Let \A_1,\dots,\A_k be symmetric n	imes n matrices and \A=\sum_i\A_i. Consider 1. \A is idempotent; 2. every \A_i is idempotent; 3. \A_i\A_j= zero for all i
e j. Any two of these imply the third. Moreover, if \A=\I_n and \sum_iank(\A_i)=n, then (ii) and (iii) hold. (ii) and (iii) imply (i): \A^2=\sum_i\A_i^2+\sum_{i
e j}\A_i\A_j=\sum_i\A_i=\A. (iii) and (ii) imply (iii): By @thm-mat-idempotent(c), 
orm{\x}^2\ge\x\T\A\x for all \x. Fix j and take \x=\A_j\mathbf{y}, so that \A_j\x=\x and \x\T\A_j\x=
orm{\x}^2. Then 
orm{\x}^2\ge\x\T\A\x=
orm{\x}^2+\sum_{i
e j}\x\T\A_i\x=
orm{\x}^2+\sum_{i
e j}
orm{\A_i\x}^2 . So \A_i\A_j\mathbf{y}=\A_i\x= zero for every i
e j and every \mathbf{y}. (iv) and (iii) imply (ii): By (iii), \A\A_i=\A_i^2. Using \A^2=\A, \A_i^2=\A\A_i=\A^2\A_i=\A\A_i^2=\A_i^3. The eigenvalues of the symmetric \A_i therefore satisfy \lambda^2=\lambda^3, so they lie in \{0,1\}, and \A_i is idempotent by @thm-mat-idempotent. For the last statement, let r_i=ank(\A_i). For each i, \I-\A_i=\sum_{j
e i}\A_j has rank at most \sum_{j
e i}r_j=n-r_i (@prp-mat-rank-product(d)). So the eigenvalue 1 of \A_i, whose eigenspace is \Null(\I-\A_i), has multiplicity at least r_i. But \A_i has exactly r_i nonzero eigenvalues, so all of them equal 1 and \A_i is idempotent. Now (i) holds trivially, and (iii) follows from the second part of the proof. The last statement is the algebraic core of Cochran’s theorem (Chapter 4): if \y\T\y=\sum_i\y\T\A_i\y and the ranks add up to n, the quadratic forms are built from mutually orthogonal projections. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \A,\B be idempotent of the same size. Show that \A\B is idempotent if \A\B=\B\A, and that \A+\B is idempotent iff \A\B+\B\A= zero. Show that the latter forces \A\B= zero (symmetry is not needed). B. Practice [B1] Let \A be idempotent. Show that \A is symmetric iff \C(\A)\perp\Null(\A). Suppose \A is symmetric. For  u=\A\x\in\C(\A) and  v\in\Null(\A),  u\T v=\x\T\A v=0. Conversely, suppose \C(\A)\perp\Null(\A). For all \x,\mathbf{y}, (\I-\A)\mathbf{y}\in\Null(\A), so \x\T\A\T(\I-\A)\mathbf{y}=0. Hence \A\T(\I-\A)= zero, that is, \A\T=\A\T\A. The right side is symmetric, so \A\T is symmetric, and so is \A.

title: 1.10 Kronecker products and the vec operator
content: Kronecker products and the vec operator Balanced designs have model matrices with a product structure, and multivariate observations have covariance matrices with one. The Kronecker product expresses both. The Kronecker product of an m\times n matrix \A and a p\times q matrix \B is the mp\times nq block matrix \A\otimes\B=(a_{ij}\B). The vec operator places the n columns of an m\times n matrix one below another, giving a vector of length mn: \vecop(\A)=(\mathbf{a}_1\T,\dots,\mathbf{a}_n\T)\T. For matrices of compatible sizes: 1. (\A\otimes\B)(\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D})=\A\mathbf{C}\otimes\B\mathbf{D} (mixed-product rule); 2. (\A\otimes\B)\T=\A\T\otimes\B\T, and (\A\otimes\B)^{-1}=\A^{-1}\otimes\B^{-1} for nonsingular \A,\B. More generally \A\ginv\otimes\B\ginv is a generalized inverse of \A\otimes\B; 3. \tr(\A\otimes\B)=\tr(\A)\tr(\B) and \rank(\A\otimes\B)=\rank(\A)\rank(\B); 4. if \A (m\times m) and \B (p\times p) are symmetric with eigenvalues \lambda_i and \mu_j, the eigenvalues of \A\otimes\B are the products \lambda_i\mu_j, and \det(\A\otimes\B)=(\det\A)^p(\det\B)^m; 5. Kronecker products of orthogonal, symmetric, idempotent, or nonnegative definite matrices are of the same kind; 6. \vecop(\A\B\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{C}\T\otimes\A)\vecop(\B) and \tr(\A\T\B)=\vecop(\A)\T\vecop(\B). (a) The (i,j) block of the left side is \sum_ka_{ik}c_{kj}\B\mathbf{D}, which is the (i,j) block of the right side. (b) Transposition is direct, and the rest follows from (a), for example (\A\otimes\B)(\A\ginv\otimes\B\ginv)(\A\otimes\B)=\A\A\ginv\A\otimes\B\B\ginv\B. (b) With \A=\mathbf{P}\bLambda\mathbf{P}\T and \B=\Q\mathbf{M}\Q\T, (a) and (b) give \A\otimes\B=(\mathbf{P}\otimes\Q)(\bLambda\otimes\mathbf{M})(\mathbf{P}\otimes\Q)\T, a spectral decomposition because \mathbf{P}\otimes\Q is orthogonal and \bLambda\otimes\mathbf{M} is diagonal with entries \lambda_i\mu_j. The determinant is the product of these. (c) The trace statement is direct. For the rank, by (a) (\A\otimes\B)(\A\ginv\otimes\B\ginv)=\A\A\ginv\otimes\B\B\ginv is idempotent with the same rank as \A\otimes\B (@prp-mat-ginverse-props(a)). Its trace is \tr(\A\A\ginv)\tr(\B\B\ginv)=\rank(\A)\rank(\B) by @prp-mat-idempotent-basic(b). (c) follows from (a), (b) and (d). (f) The jth column of \A\B\mathbf{C} is \A\B\mathbf{c}_j=\sum_kc_{kj}\A\mathbf{b}_k, which is the jth block of (\mathbf{C}\T\otimes\A)\vecop(\B). The trace identity is \sum_{ij}a_{ij}b_{ij} written two ways. The determinant formula in (d) holds for all square \A and \B, not only symmetric ones. We need only the symmetric case. [The balanced two-way layout] Let observations y_{ij}, i=1,\dots,a, j=1,\dots,b, be stacked with j running inside i. The additive model \E(y_{ij})=\mu+\alpha_i+\beta_j has model matrix \X=\bigl[\bone_a\otimes\bone_b,\ \I_a\otimes\bone_b,\ \bone_a\otimes\I_b\bigr], because \I_a\otimes\bone_b has a 1 in column i exactly for the b observations in row i. With \bar{\mathbf{J}}_k=k^{-1}\mathbf{J}_k, a symmetric idempotent averaging matrix, the mixed-product rule shows that \I_a\otimes\bar{\mathbf{J}}_b, \bar{\mathbf{J}}_a\otimes\I_b and \bar{\mathbf{J}}_a\otimes\bar{\mathbf{J}}_b replace each observation by its row mean, its column mean and the grand mean. The matrix \M=\I_a\otimes\bar{\mathbf{J}}_b+\bar{\mathbf{J}}_a\otimes\I_b-\bar{\mathbf{J}}_a\otimes\bar{\mathbf{J}}_b is symmetric and idempotent, with trace a+b-1=\rank(\X). It is the projection onto \C(\X) (Chapter 15). The script checks this for a=3 and b=4, together with each part of @prp-mat-kronecker. import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(11) def vec(M): return M.reshape(-1, order="F") # stack the columns A, B, C = rng.normal(size=(3, 4)), rng.normal(size=(4, 2)), rng.normal(size=(2, 5)) assert np.allclose(vec(A @ B @ C), np.kron(C.T, A) @ vec(B)) # vec(ABC) # balanced two-way layout: a = 3 rows, b = 4 columns, one observation per cell a, b = 3, 4 one = lambda k: np.ones((k, 1)) X = np.hstack([np.kron(one(a), one(b)), # intercept np.kron(np.eye(a), one(b)), # row indicators np.kron(one(a), np.eye(b))]) # column indicators print("rank(X) =", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X), "= a + b - 1 =", a + b - 1)

title: 1.11 Vector and matrix calculus
content:
Vector and matrix calculus Gradients of linear and quadratic functions For a differentiable scalar function f of \x\in\Real^n, the gradient \partial f/\partial\x is the column vector with entries \partial f/\partial x_i, and the Hessian \partial^2f/\partial\x\,\partial\x\T is the n	imes n matrix of second derivatives. For a vector-valued \mathbf{g}(\x)\in\Real^m, the m	imes n Jacobian \partial\mathbf{g}/\partial\x\T has (i,j) entry \partial g_i/\partial x_j. [Derivatives of linear and quadratic forms] Let \mathbf{a}\in\Real^n, let \A be n	imes n and \B be m	imes n. Then  rac{\partial(\mathbf{a}\T\x)}{\partial\x}=\mathbf{a},\qquad  rac{\partial(\B\x)}{\partial\x\T}=\B,\qquad  rac{\partial(\x\T\A\x)}{\partial\x}=(\A+\A\T)\x,\qquad  rac{\partial^2(\x\T\A\x)}{\partial\x\,\partial\x\T}=\A+\A\T . In particular \partial(\x\T\A\x)/\partial\x=2\A\x when \A is symmetric. The first two are immediate from \mathbf{a}\T\x=\sum_ia_ix_i and (\B\x)_i=\sum_jb_{ij}x_j. For the quadratic form, expand (\x+\mathbf{h})\T\A(\x+\mathbf{h})=\x\T\A\x+\mathbf{h}\T(\A+\A\T)\x+\mathbf{h}\T\A\mathbf{h} . The middle term is linear in \mathbf{h} and the last is O(
orm{\mathbf{h}}^2), so (\A+\A\T)\x is the gradient. The gradient is linear in \x with matrix \A+\A\T, which is the Hessian by the second formula. [The least squares criterion] Let S( b)=
orm{\y-\X b}^2=\y\T\y-2\y\T\X b+ b\T\X\T\X b. By @thm-mat-quadform-derivative,  rac{\partial S}{\partial b}=-2\X\T\y+2\X\T\X b=-2\X\T(\y-\X b),\qquad  rac{\partial^2S}{\partial b\,\partial b\T}=2\X\T\X . Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations \X\T\X b=\X\T\y. The Hessian is nonnegative definite, so S is convex and every solution is a global minimizer. The next result proves this without calculus, and covers the rank-deficient case. [Minimizing a quadratic function] Let \A be n	imes n nonnegative definite,  b\in\Real^n and f(\x)=\x\T\A\x-2 b\T\x. If  b\in\C(\A), the minimizers of f are exactly the solutions of \A\x= b, and the minimum value is - b\T\A\ginv b for any generalized inverse \A\ginv. If  b
otin\C(\A), then f is unbounded below. Let  b\in\C(\A) and let \x_0 solve \A\x_0= b. Completing the square, f(\x)=(\x-\x_0)\T\A(\x-\x_0)-\x_0\T\A\x_0 . The first term is nonnegative, and by @prp-mat-pd-properties(b) it is zero iff \A(\x-\x_0)= zero, that is, iff \A\x= b. The minimum is -\x_0\T\A\x_0=-\x_0\T\A\A\ginv\A\x_0=- b\T\A\ginv b. If  b
otin\C(\A), write  b= b_1+ b_2 with  b_1\in\C(\A) and  zero
e b_2\in\C(\A)\perpc=\Null(\A) (@prp-mat-complement). Then f(t b_2)=-2t
orm{ b_2}^2	o-\infty as t	o\infty. With \A=\X\T\X and  b=\X\T\y, the proposition gives least squares for every model matrix: the minimizers are the solutions of the normal equations, and the minimum of S is \y\T\y-\y\T\X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T\y. Constrained minimization To minimize a differentiable f(\x) subject to linear constraints \mathbf{H}\x=\mathbf{h}, with \mathbf{H} of size q	imes n, the method of Lagrange multipliers looks for stationary points of f(\x)+2 oldsymbol{	heta}\T(\mathbf{H}\x-\mathbf{h}) in (\x, oldsymbol{	heta}). The factor 2 is only for convenience. For quadratic f the stationary point can be written down and checked directly. Let \A be positive definite, \mathbf{H} of size q	imes n with full row rank, and f(\x)=\x\T\A\x-2 b\T\x. The unique minimizer of f subject to \mathbf{H}\x=\mathbf{h} is \x_*=\x_0-\A^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T igl(\mathbf{H}\A^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T igr)^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\x_0-\mathbf{h}), \qquad \x_0=\A^{-1} b . \mathbf{H}\A^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T is positive definite by @prp-mat-pd-properties(c,e), so \x_* is well defined, and \mathbf{H}\x_*=\mathbf{h} by direct substitution. Stationarity of the Lagrangian gives 2\A\x-2 b+2\mathbf{H}\T oldsymbol{	heta}= zero. Indeed \A\x_*- b=-\mathbf{H}\T oldsymbol{	heta}_* with  oldsymbol{	heta}_*=(\mathbf{H}\A^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T)^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\x_0-\mathbf{h}). For any feasible \x, put \mathbf{d}=\x-\x_*, so that \mathbf{H}\mathbf{d}= zero. Then f(\x)=f(\x_*)+2\mathbf{d}\T(\A\x_*- b)+\mathbf{d}\T\A\mathbf{d}=f(\x_*)-2(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{d})\T oldsymbol{	heta}_*+\mathbf{d}\T\A\mathbf{d} =f(\x_*)+\mathbf{d}\T\A\mathbf{d} , which exceeds f(\x_*) unless \mathbf{d}= zero. With \A=\X\T\X and  b=\X\T\y, this is least squares subject to a linear hypothesis \mathbf{H} beta=\mathbf{h}, the starting point of Chapter 11. Derivatives with respect to matrices and scalars Likelihoods for normal models involve \log\det Sigma and 	r( Sigma^{-1} S). For a scalar function f of an m	imes n matrix \W with functionally independent entries, \partial f/\partial\W is the m	imes n matrix with entries \partial f/\partial w_{ij}. 1. \partial	r(\A\W)/\partial\W=\A\T. 2. If \det\W>0, then \partial\log\det\W/\partial\W=(\W^{-1})\T. 3. If \A(t) is a nonsingular matrix whose entries are differentiable functions of a scalar t, with derivative \dot{\A}=\partial\A/\partial t, then  rac{\partial\A^{-1}}{\partial t}=-\A^{-1}\dot{\A}\A^{-1},\qquad  rac{\partial\log\lvert\det\Avert}{\partial t}=	r igl(\A^{-1}\dot{\A} igr). (a) 	r(\A\W)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ji}w_{ij}. (c) Differentiate \A\A^{-1}=\I by the product rule to get \dot{\A}\A^{-1}+\A\,\partial\A^{-1}/\partial t= zero. For the determinant, \A(t+h)=\A(t) igl(\I+h\A^{-1}\dot{\A}+o(h) igr). In the permutation expansion of \det(\I+h\mathbf{C}) only the diagonal product contributes terms of first order in h, so \det(\I+h\mathbf{C})=1+h	r\mathbf{C}+O(h^2). Hence \det\A(t+h)=\det\A(t) igl(1+h	r(\A^{-1}\dot{\A})+o(h) igr), and taking logarithms gives the formula. (b) Apply (c) with \A(t)=\W+t\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j\T. Then 	r(\W^{-1}\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j\T)=\mathbf{e}_j\T\W^{-1}\mathbf{e}_i, the (j,i) entry of \W^{-1}. When \W is constrained to be symmetric, w_{ij} and w_{ji} are the same variable, so the derivatives with respect to off-diagonal entries double. Some books (Rencher and Schaalje 2008) report formulas of the type 2\W^{-1}-\diag(\W^{-1}) for this reason. The simplest way to avoid the issue is to differentiate along a symmetric direction \W+t\mathbf{E}, as in (c). This is the convenient route for the normal likelihoods of Chapter 32. The listing checks the gradient formulas against central finite differences, and the script also checks part (c) and @prp-mat-quadratic-min. The largest discrepancy in the listing is 3	imes 10^{-9}, which is the size one expects from the finite-difference approximation. import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(5) p = 4 def num_grad(f, x, h=1e-6): """Central-difference gradient of a scalar function of a vector or matrix.""" g = np.zeros_like(x) for idx in np.ndindex(x.shape): e = np.zeros_like(x) e[idx] = h g[idx] = (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h) return g a = rng.normal(size=p) A = rng.normal(size=(p, p)) # not symmetric x = rng.normal(size=p) checks = { "a'x": (num_grad(lambda v: a @ v, x), a), "x'Ax": (num_grad(lambda v: v @ A @ v, x), (A + A.T) @ x), } X = rng.normal(size=(20, p)) y = rng.normal(size=20) b = rng.normal(size=p) grad_ls = -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ b) checks["||y - Xb||^2"] = (num_grad(lambda v: np.sum((y - X @ v) ** 2), b), grad_ls) S = rng.normal(size=(p, p)); S = S @ S.T + p * np.eye(p) # positive definite checks["log det S"] = (num_grad(lambda W: np.linalg.slogdet(W)[1], S), np.linalg.inv(S).T) checks["tr(AS)"] = (num_grad(lambda W: np.trace(A @ W), S), A.T) for name, (numeric, formula) in checks.items(): print(f"{name:14s} max error {np.abs(numeric - formula).max():.1e}") Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Observations fall in a clusters of size b, and  Sigma=\sigma^2\,\I_a\otimes\mathbf{E}_b, where \mathbf{E}_b=(1-ho)\I_b+ho\mathbf{J}_b. Find the eigenvalues, determinant and inverse of  Sigma using @prp-mat-kronecker, @exm-mat-equicorrelation and @exm-mat-equicorrelation-eigen. [A2] Use @prp-mat-quadratic-min to show that 
orm{\y-\X b}^2+\lambda
orm{ b}^2 with \lambda>0 has the unique minimizer (\X\T\X+\lambda\I)^{-1}\X\T\y, whatever the rank of \X. B. Practice [B1] Let \X have full column rank, \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\y, and let \mathbf{H} be q	imes p with full row rank. Show that the minimizer of 
orm{\y-\X b}^2 subject to \mathbf{H} b=\mathbf{h} is \hbeta_H=\hbeta-(\X\T\X)^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h}),\qquad \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{H}(\X\T\X)^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T, and that the increase in the residual sum of squares is (\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h})\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h}). Apply @prp-mat-lagrange with \A=\X\T\X and  b=\X\T\y. Since 
orm{\y-\X b}^2=\y\T\y+f( b) and \x_0=\hbeta, this gives \hbeta_H. By completing the square as in @prp-mat-quadratic-min, 
orm{\y-\X b}^2=
orm{\y-\X\hbeta}^2+( b-\hbeta)\T\X\T\X( b-\hbeta) for every  b. With  b-\hbeta=-(\X\T\X)^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h}), the increase is (\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h})\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}\mathbf{H}(\X\T\X)^{-1}\mathbf{H}\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h}) =(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h})\T\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{H}\hbeta-\mathbf{h}). This quadratic form is the numerator of the F statistic in Chapter 11 (@thm-glh-general-f).

title: 1.12 Summary and Notes
content: Summary and Notes Summary 1. Row rank equals column rank, and \rank(\A)+\dim\Null(\A) is the number of columns. \C(\A\T\A)=\C(\A\T), so the normal equations are always consistent (@thm-mat-row-col-rank, @thm-mat-rank-nullity and @prp-mat-rank-product). 2. A generalized inverse satisfies \A\A\ginv\A=\A. Every matrix has one, built from any nonsingular r\times r submatrix. The Moore–Penrose inverse is the unique one that is also reflexive and makes \A\A^+ and \A^+\A symmetric (@def-mat-ginverse, @thm-mat-ginverse-exists, @prp-mat-nonsingular-submatrix and @def-mat-moore-penrose). 3. \A\x=\bb is consistent iff \A\A\ginv\bb=\bb, and then its solutions are \A\ginv\bb+(\I-\A\ginv\A)\bz. A linear function \mathbf{q}\T\x is the same for all solutions iff \mathbf{q}\in\C(\A\T) (@thm-mat-consistency and @cor-mat-invariant). 4. Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles. Gram–Schmidt gives the QR factorization, and \Real^n=\C(\A\T)\dirsum\Null(\A) (@prp-mat-orthogonal, @thm-mat-qr and @prp-mat-complement). 5. \tr(\A\B)=\tr(\B\A). Block elimination gives the determinant and inverse of a partitioned matrix through Schur complements, and the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury identity as a special case (@thm-mat-trace-cyclic, @thm-mat-block-determinant, @thm-mat-partitioned-inverse and @thm-mat-woodbury). 6. A symmetric matrix is \Q\bLambda\Q\T with \Q orthogonal. Positive definiteness is equivalent to positive eigenvalues, to a Cholesky factorization, and to positive leading minors. Nonnegative definite matrices have a unique nonnegative definite square root (@thm-mat-spectral, @thm-mat-pd-characterizations and @thm-mat-square-root). 7. The Rayleigh quotient \x\T\A\x/\x\T\x ranges over [\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}] (@thm-mat-extremal-rayleigh and @cor-mat-generalized-rayleigh). 8. Every matrix is \bU\bD\V\T. The condition number \kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} bounds error growth, is squared by forming \X\T\X, and its smallest singular vector exhibits near-dependences among the columns (@thm-mat-svd, @def-mat-condition-number and @prp-mat-svd-norms). 9. Idempotent matrices have eigenvalues 0 and 1 and rank equal to trace. Symmetric ones are \Q_1\Q_1\T. If symmetric matrices summing to \I have ranks summing to n, they are idempotent and mutually orthogonal (@prp-mat-idempotent-basic, @thm-mat-idempotent and @thm-mat-idempotent-sum). 10. Kronecker products factor balanced designs. \vecop(\A\B\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{C}\T\otimes\A)\vecop(\B) (@prp-mat-kronecker). 11. \partial(\x\T\A\x)/\partial\x=(\A+\A\T)\x. Quadratic functions with nonnegative definite matrices are minimized by solving a linear system, with or without linear constraints (@thm-mat-quadform-derivative, @prp-mat-quadratic-min and @prp-mat-lagrange). Notes and sources Coverage and framing. The selection of results follows what the rest of the book uses. Rencher and Schaalje (2008, chapter 2) was the checklist for topics: its sections on positive definite matrices, generalized inverses, orthogonal matrices, idempotent matrices and matrix calculus correspond to Section 1.7, Section 1.3, Section 1.5, Section 1.9 and Section 1.11. Several results that Rencher and Schaalje state without proof or with a reference, such as the general solution of a consistent system, the characterizations of positive definiteness and the sums of idempotent matrices, are proved here. The vector-space point of view, in which column spaces, null spaces and orthogonal complements come first and matrices second, is that of Christensen (2020, appendices A and B). Seber and Lee (2003, appendix A) is a compact list of further matrix facts. The Kronecker product results in Section 1.10 are also in Christensen’s appendix B. Linear algebra for statisticians. Harville (1997) is the most complete treatment written for statisticians, with full proofs of the determinant facts assumed in @prp-mat-det and a long development of generalized inverses. Searle (1982) is more elementary and has many worked examples from linear models. Horn and Johnson (2013) is the standard reference for eigenvalue inequalities, positive definite matrices and norms. Halmos (1958) gives the coordinate-free view of the vector-space facts used in Section 1.2. Generalized inverses. The four conditions of @def-mat-moore-penrose are due to Penrose (1955), who proved existence and uniqueness. E. H. Moore had described an equivalent inverse decades earlier. Rao (1973) made the weaker inverse \A\A\ginv\A=\A the basic tool of linear-model theory, and it is his approach that Section 1.4 and Chapter 8 follow. The construction from a nonsingular submatrix in @thm-mat-ginverse-exists is a matrix-free way of stating an algorithm that is often given as a sequence of steps (Searle 1982). Schur complements and updating formulas. The name “Schur complement” and the notation for it vary. Zhang (2005) collects the history and many applications. The rank-one formula @eq-mat-sherman-morrison is from Sherman and Morrison (1950), and the general identity @eq-mat-woodbury from Woodbury (1950). Henderson and Searle (1981) trace earlier appearances and compare several derivations. Obtaining the identity by comparing two expressions for one block of a partitioned inverse, as in @thm-mat-woodbury, is a classical route. Singular values and conditioning. Stewart (1993) tells the early history of the singular value decomposition, beginning with Beltrami and Jordan in the 1870s. The low-rank approximation theorem, @prp-mat-svd-norms(c) and its Frobenius form, is usually credited to Eckart and Young (1936), although Stewart points out that Schmidt had proved it earlier in the setting of integral equations. Golub and Van Loan (2013) is the reference for computing the decomposition and for perturbation bounds such as @eq-mat-perturbation, and Higham (2002) for their refinements. The use of scaled condition numbers and singular vectors to diagnose collinearity is due to Belsley et al. (1980). Chapter 26 returns to it. Kronecker products and calculus. Henderson and Searle (1979) survey the vec operator and its uses in multivariate statistics. Magnus and Neudecker (2019) develop matrix calculus systematically through differentials, which avoid the bookkeeping of the entrywise definitions used in Section 1.11 and handle symmetric matrix arguments cleanly. title: Random Vectors: Expectation and Covariance Operators
content: Random Vectors: Expectation and Covariance Operators A linear model is a statement about the first two moments of a random vector: its mean lies in a subspace and its covariance matrix has a given form. This chapter builds the calculus for such statements. Expectation and covariance become matrix operators that commute with linear maps, covariance matrices turn out to be exactly the nonnegative definite matrices, and a singular covariance means the vector is confined to a flat. The mean of a quadratic form needs only two moments; its variance needs four. Partitioning a vector gives cross-covariances, Schur complements and the best linear predictor, which foreshadow conditional distributions under normality. What you need. Chapter 1 (trace, spectral theorem, nonnegative definite matrices and their square roots, generalized inverses, partitioned matrices), and probability at the level of expectations, variances and independence of random variables. Roadmap - Mean vectors and covariance matrices - Linear and affine transformations - Expectation of quadratic forms - Correlation matrices - Moments of partitioned random vectors - Moment generating functions and independence - Sample moments and their computation - Summary and notes

title: 2.1 Mean vectors and covariance matrices
content:
Mean vectors and covariance matrices Random vectors enter regression in two different ways. The first is the response vector. In the model \Y=\X beta+ e, \Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\T has one entry per observational unit, and so does the unobservable error  e. The assumptions that do the real work in Chapter 5, Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 are not about the shape of any distribution. They are statements about moments: \E( e)= zero, and the errors have equal variances and are uncorrelated. The second way is the measurement vector. When several quantities are recorded on the same unit, such as income, age and years of schooling, the unit contributes a vector whose components are usually correlated and measured in different units. Random regressors, errors-in-variables models and multivariate responses are all built from such vectors. Both uses need the same toolkit: expectation and covariance as operations on vectors and matrices, their behaviour under linear maps, and the expected values of quadratic forms. Throughout, a random vector has finite second moments if every component has finite variance. Random matrices and their expectation [Expectation of a random matrix] A random matrix \mathbf{Z}=(Z_{ij}) is an m	imes k array of random variables. If every Z_{ij} has a finite expectation, the expectation of \mathbf{Z} is the m	imes k matrix of expectations, \E(\mathbf{Z})= igl(\E(Z_{ij}) igr). A random vector is the case k=1. The definition works entry by entry, so every rule that is linear in the entries carries over at once. [Linearity of expectation] Let \mathbf{Z} and \mathbf{Z}_2 be m	imes k random matrices with integrable entries, and let \A (l	imes m), \B (k	imes s) and \mathbf{C} (l	imes s) be constant matrices. Then 1. \E(\A\mathbf{Z}\B+\mathbf{C})=\A\,\E(\mathbf{Z})\,\B+\mathbf{C}; 2. \E(\mathbf{Z}+\mathbf{Z}_2)=\E(\mathbf{Z})+\E(\mathbf{Z}_2) and \E(\mathbf{Z}\T)=\E(\mathbf{Z})\T; 3. if m=k, then \E	r(\mathbf{Z})=	r\E(\mathbf{Z}). The (i,j) entry of \A\mathbf{Z}\B+\mathbf{C} is \sum_{r}\sum_{t}a_{ir}Z_{rt}b_{tj}+c_{ij}, a finite linear combination of integrable random variables with constant coefficients. Its expectation is \sum_r\sum_t a_{ir}\E(Z_{rt})b_{tj}+c_{ij}, which is the (i,j) entry of \A\E(\mathbf{Z})\B+\mathbf{C}. Parts (b) and (c) are the same argument applied to Z_{ij}+Z_{2,ij}, to Z_{ji}, and to \sum_iZ_{ii}. Two warnings go with this proposition. The multipliers must be constant: if \A is random, \E(\A\mathbf{Z}) is generally not \E(\A)\E(\mathbf{Z}). And the expectation of a product of random matrices is generally not the product of expectations. It is when every entry of the first is independent of every entry of the second, because then \E(Z_{ir}W_{rj})=\E(Z_{ir})\E(W_{rj}) for each term. Mean vector and covariance matrix [Mean vector and covariance matrices] Let \Y be a p	imes1 random vector with finite second moments. Its mean vector is  mu=\E(\Y), and its covariance matrix is the p	imes p matrix \Cov(\Y)=\E igl[(\Y- mu)(\Y- mu)\T igr], whose (i,j) entry is \sigma_{ij}=\Cov(Y_i,Y_j) and whose diagonal holds the variances \sigma_{ii}=\Var(Y_i). If  U (p	imes1) and \V (q	imes1) both have finite second moments, their cross-covariance matrix is the p	imes q matrix \Cov( U,\V)=\E igl[( U-\E U)(\V-\E\V)\T igr], with (i,j) entry \Cov(U_i,V_j). The expectations exist: \lvert U_iV_jvert\le	frac12(U_i^2+V_j^2), so finite second moments make every product integrable. We often write  Sigma for \Cov(\Y), and \Cov(\Y)=\Cov(\Y,\Y). Some books write \Var(\Y) or D(\Y) for the covariance matrix. We keep \Var for scalars. The symbol \Cov then has three uses: \Cov(Y_i,Y_j) is a number, \Cov(\Y) is a symmetric square matrix, and \Cov( U,\V) is a rectangular matrix that is usually not symmetric even when p=q. [Elementary properties] Let \Y,  U, \V have finite second moments, with  mu=\E(\Y) and  Sigma=\Cov(\Y), and let \mathbf{a},  b be constant vectors of matching sizes. Then: 1.  Sigma is symmetric; 2. \Cov( U,\V)=\E( U\V\T)-\E( U)\E(\V)\T, and in particular  Sigma=\E(\Y\Y\T)- mu mu\T; 3. \Cov(\V, U)=\Cov( U,\V)\T; 4. \Cov( U+\mathbf{a},\V+ b)=\Cov( U,\V); 5. \E igl[(\Y-\mathbf{a})(\Y-\mathbf{a})\T igr]= Sigma+( mu-\mathbf{a})( mu-\mathbf{a})\T, and hence \E
orm{\Y-\mathbf{a}}^2=	r( Sigma)+
orm{ mu-\mathbf{a}}^2. (a) and (c) hold because (\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}\T)\T=\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}\T and expectation commutes with transposition. For (b), expand ( U- mu_U)(\V- mu_V)\T= U\V\T- U mu_V\T- mu_U\V\T+ mu_U mu_V\T and take expectations with @prp-rv-expectation-linear. The two middle terms each give - mu_U mu_V\T. (d) holds because adding a constant does not change the centred vectors. For (e), write \Y-\mathbf{a}=(\Y- mu)+( mu-\mathbf{a}) and expand. The cross terms contain the factor \E(\Y- mu)= zero and vanish. The trace identity follows from 
orm{\mathbf{v}}^2=	r(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}\T) and @prp-rv-expectation-linear(c). Part (e) is the vector form of “mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias”. It shows that the mean is the constant vector closest to \Y in expected squared distance, and that the minimal value is 	r( Sigma)=\sum_i\Var(Y_i). The matrix statement is stronger than the trace statement. It says that the second-moment matrix about any point exceeds  Sigma by a nonnegative definite matrix of rank at most one. Uncorrelated is not independent Random vectors  U and \V are uncorrelated if \Cov( U,\V)= zero. If  U and \V are independent, then \E(U_iV_j)=\E(U_i)\E(V_j) for all i,j, so they are uncorrelated. The converse is false, and it fails in the most innocent-looking cases. [A point on a circle] Let \Theta be uniform on [0,2\pi) and \Y=(\cos\Theta,\sin\Theta)\T. Then \E(\cos\Theta)=\E(\sin\Theta)=0, \E(\cos^2\Theta)=\E(\sin^2\Theta)=	frac12, and \E(\cos\Theta\sin\Theta)=	frac12\E(\sin2\Theta)=0. So  mu= zero and \Cov(\Y)=	frac12\I_2, exactly the moments of two independent coordinates. Yet Y_1^2+Y_2^2=1: once Y_1 is known, Y_2 is known up to sign. Covariance measures linear association only, and the dependence here is entirely nonlinear. For jointly normal vectors, zero covariance and independence coincide (@thm-mvn-independence). That equivalence rests on joint normality, not on normal marginals, and it is one of the main reasons normal theory is so tractable. Scalar summaries. The total variance 	r( Sigma) ignores correlation; the generalized variance \det( Sigma) does not. If \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p are the eigenvalues of  Sigma (@thm-mat-spectral), these are \sum_i\lambda_i and \prod_i\lambda_i, and both are unchanged by a rotation \Y\mapsto\Q\Y. The determinant can be tiny even when every variance is large, if one eigenvalue is near zero. @thm-rv-cov-nnd shows that a zero eigenvalue means some linear combination of \Y does not vary at all. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \mathbf{Z} be an n	imes p random matrix whose entries are independent, with mean 0 and variance \sigma^2. Show that \E(\mathbf{Z}\T\mathbf{Z})=n\sigma^2\I_p and \E(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}\T)=p\sigma^2\I_n. For a constant p	imes p matrix \B, find \E(\mathbf{Z}\B\mathbf{Z}\T). B. Practice [B1] Let X have a distribution symmetric about 0 with \Var(X)=1 and \E X^4<\infty, let S be independent of X with \Pr(S=1)=\Pr(S=-1)=	frac12, and put \Y=(X,SX)\T. Show that the two components have the same distribution and are uncorrelated, and that \Cov(Y_1^2,Y_2^2)=\Var(X^2). Deduce that Y_1 and Y_2 are independent iff X is itself a random sign. (Chapter 3 takes X standard normal.) Since S is independent of X and X is symmetric, \Pr(SX\le y)=	frac12\Pr(X\le y)+	frac12\Pr(-X\le y)=\Pr(X\le y). By independence, \Cov(X,SX)=\E(S)\E(X^2)=0. Both squares equal X^2, so \Cov(Y_1^2,Y_2^2)=\Var(X^2). Functions of independent variables are independent, hence uncorrelated, so \Var(X^2)>0 makes Y_1 and Y_2 dependent. If \Var(X^2)=0, then X^2=\E X^2=1 with probability one, and by symmetry X=\pm1 with probability 	frac12 each. Then \Pr(Y_1=a,Y_2=b)=\Pr(X=a)\Pr(S=ab)=	frac14 for all signs a,b, which is the product of the marginal probabilities, as in @exm-rv-pairwise. [B2] Show that \E igl[(\Y-\mathbf{a})(\Y-\mathbf{a})\T igr]-\Cov(\Y) is nonnegative definite for every constant \mathbf{a}, with equality iff \mathbf{a}= mu. Deduce that \mathbf{a}= mu minimizes \E igl[(\Y-\mathbf{a})\T\mathbf{N}(\Y-\mathbf{a}) igr] for every positive definite \mathbf{N}.

title: 2.2 Linear and affine transformations
content:
Linear and affine transformations Almost every statistic in a linear model is a linear function of the response: least squares coefficients, fitted values, residuals, contrasts. Their means and covariance matrices follow from one theorem. The transformation rules [Moments of affine transformations] Let \Y be a p	imes1 random vector with finite second moments, \E(\Y)= mu and \Cov(\Y)= Sigma. Let \A be k	imes p, \B be m	imes p, and  b be k	imes1, all constant. Then 1. \E(\A\Y+ b)=\A mu+ b; 2. \Cov(\A\Y+ b)=\A Sigma\A\T; 3. \Cov(\A\Y,\B\Y)=\A Sigma\B\T. More generally, if  U and \V have finite second moments and \A, \B,  b, \mathbf{c} are constants of conformable sizes, then \Cov(\A U+ b,\,\B\V+\mathbf{c})=\A\,\Cov( U,\V)\,\B\T. (a) is @prp-rv-expectation-linear(a). For the general statement, the centred vectors are \A U+ b-\E(\A U+ b)=\A( U-\E U) and similarly \B(\V-\E\V). Hence \Cov(\A U+ b,\B\V+\mathbf{c}) =\E igl[\A( U-\E U)(\V-\E\V)\T\B\T igr] =\A\,\E igl[( U-\E U)(\V-\E\V)\T igr]\B\T , again by @prp-rv-expectation-linear(a). Parts (c) and (b) are the cases  U=\V=\Y, and \B=\A in (b). For a single linear combination, \A=\mathbf{a}\T is a row vector, and (b) and (c) give \Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y)=\mathbf{a}\T Sigma\mathbf{a}=\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p a_ia_j\sigma_{ij}, \qquad \Cov(\mathbf{a}\T\Y, b\T\Y)=\mathbf{a}\T Sigma b . {#eq-rv-linear-combination} Every variance and covariance enters \Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y), weighted by the products of the coefficients. Conversely,  Sigma is determined by the variances of linear combinations, because \sigma_{ij}=	frac12[\Var(Y_i+Y_j)-\Var(Y_i)-\Var(Y_j)]. [Covariance of sums] Let  U, U_2,\V have finite second moments, with  U and  U_2 of the same size in (a), and  U and \V of the same size in (b). Then 1. \Cov( U+ U_2,\V)=\Cov( U,\V)+\Cov( U_2,\V); 2. \Cov( U+\V)=\Cov( U)+\Cov( U,\V)+\Cov(\V, U)+\Cov(\V); 3. if \Y_1,\dots,\Y_n are pairwise uncorrelated p	imes1 vectors and c_1,\dots,c_n are constants, then \Cov igl(\sum_ic_i\Y_i igr)=\sum_ic_i^2\Cov(\Y_i). In particular, if every \Cov(\Y_i)= Sigma, then \Cov( ar{\Y})= Sigma/n. (a) Centre each vector and use linearity of the outer product and of \E. (b) Apply (a) in each argument; note that the two cross terms are transposes of each other, not equal. (b) By (a) and (b), applied repeatedly, \Cov igl(\sum_ic_i\Y_i igr)=\sum_i\sum_jc_ic_j\Cov(\Y_i,\Y_j), using \Cov(c U,\V)=c\Cov( U,\V) from @thm-rv-linear. The terms with i
e j vanish. [Centring a sample] Let \Y be n	imes1 with \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I_n, and write \mathbf{J}= one one\T. The mean is  ar{Y}=n^{-1} one\T\Y, and the vector of deviations is \mathbf{d}=(\I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J})\Y. The matrix \I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J} is symmetric and idempotent, so @thm-rv-linear gives \Cov(\mathbf{d})=\sigma^2(\I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J}), \qquad \Cov( ar{Y},\mathbf{d})=\sigma^2 n^{-1} one\T(\I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J})= zero\T . The deviations have variances \sigma^2(1-1/n) and are negatively correlated, with correlation -1/(n-1) between each pair, because they are forced to sum to zero. And each deviation is uncorrelated with the mean. Under normality, uncorrelated becomes independent (@exm-mvn-mean-deviations), which is the first half of @cor-qf-sample-variance. Covariance matrices are nonnegative definite A variance cannot be negative, and by @eq-rv-linear-combination this simple fact constrains the whole matrix. Recall from @def-mat-nnd that a symmetric  Sigma is nonnegative definite if \mathbf{a}\T Sigma\mathbf{a}\ge0 for all \mathbf{a}, and positive definite if in addition \mathbf{a}\T Sigma\mathbf{a}>0 for \mathbf{a}
e zero. [Covariance matrices] Let \Y have finite second moments, mean  mu and covariance matrix  Sigma. 1.  Sigma is nonnegative definite. 2. Conversely, every p	imes p nonnegative definite matrix is the covariance matrix of some random vector. 3. For a constant \mathbf{a},  Sigma\mathbf{a}= zero iff \mathbf{a}\T\Y=\mathbf{a}\T mu with probability one. 4. \Pr(\Y- mu\in\C( Sigma))=1. If \mathcal S is any subspace with \Pr(\Y- mu\in\mathcal S)=1, then \C( Sigma)\subseteq\mathcal S. In particular,  Sigma is singular iff some nontrivial linear combination of \Y is constant with probability one. Then \Y lies, with probability one, in the affine subspace  mu+\C( Sigma) of dimension ank( Sigma)<p, and this is the smallest such flat. (a)  Sigma is symmetric, and \mathbf{a}\T Sigma\mathbf{a}=\Var(\mathbf{a}\T\Y)\ge0 by @eq-rv-linear-combination. (b) Let  Sigma be nonnegative definite and let  Sigma^{1/2} be its symmetric nonnegative definite square root (@thm-mat-square-root). Let \Z have independent components with mean 0 and variance 1, for instance independent standard normal variables, so that \Cov(\Z)=\I. Then \Cov( Sigma^{1/2}\Z)= Sigma^{1/2}\I Sigma^{1/2}= Sigma. (c) If  Sigma\mathbf{a}= zero, the random variable \mathbf{a}\T(\Y- mu) has mean zero and variance \mathbf{a}\T Sigma\mathbf{a}=0, so it is zero with probability one. Conversely, if \mathbf{a}\T(\Y- mu)=0 with probability one, then  Sigma\mathbf{a}=\E igl[(\Y- mu)\,(\Y- mu)\T\mathbf{a} igr]= zero. (d) Let \mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_s be a basis of \Null( Sigma). By (c), each event \{\mathbf{a}_j\T(\Y- mu)=0\} has probability one, and so does their intersection. On that intersection \Y- mu is orthogonal to \Null( Sigma). Because  Sigma is symmetric, \Null( Sigma) is the orthogonal complement of \C( Sigma), and so \Y- mu\in\C( Sigma). Now let \mathcal S be a subspace with \Pr(\Y- mu\in\mathcal S)=1. For every \mathbf{a}\in\mathcal S\perpc we have \mathbf{a}\T(\Y- mu)=0 with probability one, hence \mathbf{a}\in\Null( Sigma)=\C( Sigma)\perpc by (c). So \mathcal S\perpc\subseteq\C( Sigma)\perpc, and taking orthogonal complements gives \C( Sigma)\subseteq\mathcal S. The final statements follow, with \dim\C( Sigma)=ank( Sigma). For minimality among all flats, suppose \Pr(\Y\in\mathbf{c}+\mathcal S)=1 for a vector \mathbf{c} and a subspace \mathcal S. Every \mathbf{a}\in\mathcal S\perpc has \mathbf{a}\T(\Y-\mathbf{c})=0 with probability one, and taking expectations gives \mathbf{a}\T( mu-\mathbf{c})=0. Hence  mu-\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal S, so \mathbf{c}+\mathcal S= mu+\mathcal S, and the subspace case applies. A covariance matrix is therefore positive definite exactly when no linear combination of the components is degenerate. Singular covariance matrices are not pathological. They arise whenever the components satisfy an exact linear constraint, as with the deviations of @exm-rv-centering, whose covariance matrix has rank n-1 because  one\T\mathbf{d}=0. The residual vector of a regression is another case: it is orthogonal to every column of \X, and when \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I its covariance matrix has rank n-ank(\X) (Section 2.2, Chapter 6). [Multinomial counts] In m independent trials, each outcome falls into one of k categories with probabilities  oldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_k)\T, where \sum_j\pi_j=1. Let \mathbf{Z}_t be the indicator vector of trial t, with a single 1 in the position of its category. Then \E(\mathbf{Z}_t)= oldsymbol{\pi}, and \mathbf{Z}_t\mathbf{Z}_t\T=\diag(\mathbf{Z}_t) because the indicator has only one nonzero entry. So \Cov(\mathbf{Z}_t)=\diag( oldsymbol{\pi})- oldsymbol{\pi} oldsymbol{\pi}\T. The count vector \Y=\sum_t\mathbf{Z}_t is a sum of independent vectors, and @prp-rv-sums(c) gives  Sigma=\Cov(\Y)=m igl(\diag( oldsymbol{\pi})- oldsymbol{\pi} oldsymbol{\pi}\T igr). Because  Sigma one=m( oldsymbol{\pi}- oldsymbol{\pi}\, oldsymbol{\pi}\T one)= zero, the matrix is singular, and @thm-rv-cov-nnd(c) recovers the constraint  one\T\Y=m. For m=20 and  oldsymbol{\pi}=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\T the eigenvalues are 7.762, 4.638 and 0. All 5000 simulated count vectors lie in the plane  mu+\C( Sigma)=\{\y: one\T\y=m\}. Linear maps cannot increase the rank of a covariance matrix, since ank(\A Sigma\A\T)\leank( Sigma) (@exr-rv-cov-rank). They can, however, discard degenerate directions. If \Y=(Z,Z)\T with \Var(Z)=1, then  Sigma has all entries equal to 1 and is singular, while \A=(1,0) gives \Var(\A\Y)=1>0. By @thm-rv-linear, the covariance matrix of \A\Y is \A Sigma\A\T. If  Sigma is positive definite and \A has full row rank k\le p, then for \mathbf{b}
eq zero the vector \A\T\mathbf{b} is nonzero and \mathbf{b}\T\A Sigma\A\T\mathbf{b}>0. So \A Sigma\A\T is positive definite. If k>p, then \A Sigma\A\T has rank at most p and is singular. A vector of more than p linear combinations of p variables always satisfies a linear constraint. Standardization and Mahalanobis distance A scalar with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2>0 is standardized by (Y-\mu)/\sigma. The vector version must remove correlation as well as scale. [Whitening] Let  Sigma=\Cov(\Y) be positive definite, with \E(\Y)= mu. 1. \Z= Sigma^{-1/2}(\Y- mu) has \E(\Z)= zero and \Cov(\Z)=\I_p. 2. A p	imes p matrix \W satisfies \W Sigma\W\T=\I_p iff \W=\Q Sigma^{-1/2} for some orthogonal \Q. In particular, if  Sigma= L L\T is the Cholesky factorization, \W= L^{-1} is such a matrix. 3. For every \W as in (b), 
orm{\W(\Y- mu)}^2=(\Y- mu)\T Sigma^{-1}(\Y- mu). (a) By @thm-rv-linear, \Cov(\Z)= Sigma^{-1/2} Sigma Sigma^{-1/2}=\I, since  Sigma^{-1/2} is symmetric and commutes with  Sigma. (b) If \W=\Q Sigma^{-1/2}, then \W Sigma\W\T=\Q\Q\T=\I. Conversely, if \W Sigma\W\T=\I, put \Q=\W Sigma^{1/2}. Then \Q\Q\T=\W Sigma\W\T=\I, so the square matrix \Q is orthogonal, and \W=\Q Sigma^{-1/2}. For the Cholesky factor,  L^{-1} Sigma( L\T)^{-1}= L^{-1} L L\T( L\T)^{-1}=\I. (c) \W\T\W= Sigma^{-1/2}\Q\T\Q Sigma^{-1/2}= Sigma^{-1}. The quantity in (c), \Delta^2(\Y)=(\Y- mu)\T Sigma^{-1}(\Y- mu), {#eq-rv-mahalanobis} is the squared Mahalanobis distance of \Y from  mu. It measures distance in units of the covariance structure. Its level sets are ellipsoids with axes along the eigenvectors of  Sigma, with half-lengths proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues. Whitening maps these ellipsoids to spheres. Part (b) says that whitening is unique only up to a rotation or reflection. Different choices give different coordinates, but the same distances. [Two whitenings] Take  mu=(3,1)\T and  Sigma= egin{psmallmatrix}4&2.4\2.4&2.25\end{psmallmatrix}, so the standard deviations are 2 and 1.5 and the correlation is 0.8. The eigenvalues are 5.680 and 0.570. The symmetric and Cholesky whitening matrices are  Sigma^{-1/2}= egin{pmatrix}0.717&-0.425\-0.425&1.027\end{pmatrix}, \qquad  L^{-1}= egin{pmatrix}0.500&0\-0.667&1.111\end{pmatrix}. The Cholesky version standardizes Y_1 alone and then removes from Y_2 its linear dependence on Y_1, in the spirit of Gram–Schmidt. The symmetric version treats both coordinates alike and moves points as little as possible (@exr-rv-whitening-closest). Figure 2.2.1 applies both to 400 simulated points. The two whitened clouds differ by a rotation through 22.5^\circ, and every point keeps its Mahalanobis distance. [Figure 2.2.1. Whitening a correlated sample. (a) Draws with \Cov(\Y)= Sigma and the Mahalanobis contours \Delta=1,2,3. (b) The symmetric whitening  Sigma^{-1/2}(\Y- mu). (c) The Cholesky whitening  L^{-1}(\Y- mu). The contours become circles in both, and the three coloured points keep their distance from the origin. Panels (b) and (c) differ by a rotation (@prp-rv-whitening).] Figure 2.2.1. Whitening a correlated sample. (a) Draws with \Cov(\Y)= Sigma and the Mahalanobis contours \Delta=1,2,3. (b) The symmetric whitening  Sigma^{-1/2}(\Y- mu). (c) The Cholesky whitening  L^{-1}(\Y- mu). The contours become circles in both, and the three coloured points keep their distance from the origin. Panels (b) and (c) differ by a rotation (@prp-rv-whitening). [Whitening a correlated sample. (a) Draws with \Cov(\Y)= Sigma and the Mahalanobis contours \Delta=1,2,3. (b) The symmetric whitening  Sigma^{-1/2}(\Y- mu). (c) The Cholesky whitening  L^{-1}(\Y- mu). The contours become circles in both, and the three coloured points keep their distance from the origin. Panels (b) and (c) differ by a rotation (@prp-rv-whitening).] Whitening a correlated sample. (a) Draws with \Cov(\Y)= Sigma and the Mahalanobis contours \Delta=1,2,3. (b) The symmetric whitening  Sigma^{-1/2}(\Y- mu). (c) The Cholesky whitening  L^{-1}(\Y- mu). The contours become circles in both, and the three coloured points keep their distance from the origin. Panels (b) and (c) differ by a rotation (@prp-rv-whitening). import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(2) mu = np.array([3.0, 1.0]) Sigma = np.array([[4.0, 2.4], [2.4, 2.25]]) # correlation 2.4 / (2 * 1.5) = 0.8 lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma) # spectral decomposition W_sym = U @ np.diag(lam ** -0.5) @ U.T # Sigma^{-1/2} L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma) # Sigma = L L', L lower triangular W_chol = np.linalg.inv(L) # L^{-1} n = 400 Y = mu + rng.standard_normal((n, 2)) @ L.T # any draws with Cov = Sigma will do Z_sym = (Y - mu) @ W_sym.T Z_chol = (Y - mu) @ W_chol.T Q = W_chol @ np.linalg.inv(W_sym) # L^{-1} Sigma^{1/2} print("Q'Q =", np.round(Q.T @ Q, 12)) Whitening runs in both directions. If \Cov(\Z)=\I, then  mu+ Sigma^{1/2}\Z, or  mu+ L\Z, has mean  mu and covariance  Sigma. This is how correlated vectors are simulated, and with \Z standard normal it is how Chapter 3 constructs \Normal_p( mu, Sigma). The Mahalanobis distance then appears in the exponent of the density (@thm-mvn-density). When  Sigma is singular, no matrix whitens all of \Y, since a degenerate combination cannot be scaled to variance one. The best one can do is whiten within the support  mu+\C( Sigma) using the Moore–Penrose inverse square root (@exr-rv-singular-whitening). Second moments in the linear model Here is how the rules of this section enter regression. Suppose \Y=\X beta+ e with \X an n	imes p constant matrix of rank p, \E( e)= zero and \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\I_n. Adding the constant \X beta changes the mean but not the covariance, so \E(\Y)=\X beta and \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I_n. The least squares estimator \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y is \A\Y with \A=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T, so \E(\hbeta)=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\X beta= beta, \qquad \Cov(\hbeta)=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}. No distributional assumption was used, and none is needed for the Gauss–Markov theorem (@thm-opt-gauss-markov). Fitted values and residuals are also linear in \Y, and their covariance matrices are computed the same way in Chapter 5 and Chapter 6. If instead \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\V with \V positive definite, then \V^{-1/2}\Y=\V^{-1/2}\X beta+\V^{-1/2} e is a model with \Cov(\V^{-1/2} e)=\sigma^2\I. Whitening the data turns correlated errors back into the standard case. This is generalized least squares, which Chapter 6 and Chapter 31 develop. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I_3. Find the covariance and correlation matrices of the successive differences (Y_2-Y_1,\,Y_3-Y_2)\T, and of (Y_2-Y_1,\,Y_3-Y_2,\,Y_3-Y_1)\T. Which is singular, and which linear combination is degenerate? [A2] For p=2 and  Sigma= L L\T, show that the second component of  L^{-1}(\Y- mu) is a multiple of Y_2-\mu_2-(\sigma_{12}/\sigma_{11})(Y_1-\mu_1). Explain the connection with @thm-rv-blp. B. Practice [B1] Let \varepsilon_0,\dots,\varepsilon_n be uncorrelated with variance \sigma^2, and let Y_t=\varepsilon_t+	heta\varepsilon_{t-1} for t=1,\dots,n. Find \Cov(\Y), and show that it is positive definite for every real 	heta, including 	heta=\pm1. \Y=\A e, where \A is n	imes(n+1) with 	heta in column t and 1 in column t+1 of row t (columns indexed by \varepsilon_0,\dots,\varepsilon_n). So \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\A\A\T is tridiagonal, with \sigma^2(1+	heta^2) on the diagonal and \sigma^2	heta next to it. The last n columns of \A form a lower bidiagonal matrix with unit diagonal, which is nonsingular. So \A has full row rank n, and \A\A\T is positive definite (Section 2.2) whatever the value of 	heta. [B2] Show that \C(\A Sigma\A\T)=\C(\A Sigma) for every nonnegative definite  Sigma and conformable \A. Deduce that ank\Cov(\A\Y)\leank\Cov(\Y). [B3] Let  Sigma be positive definite. Among all \W with \W Sigma\W\T=\I, show that \E
orm{\W(\Y- mu)-(\Y- mu)}^2 is minimized uniquely by \W= Sigma^{-1/2}. Hint: use @prp-rv-whitening(b) and show that 	r(\Q Sigma^{1/2})\le	r( Sigma^{1/2}) for orthogonal \Q. Write \W=\Q Sigma^{-1/2}. By @cor-rv-quadform-special(a) with \A=(\W-\I)\T(\W-\I), \E
orm{(\W-\I)(\Y- mu)}^2=	r igl((\W-\I) Sigma(\W-\I)\T igr) =	r(\W Sigma\W\T)-2	r(\W Sigma)+	r( Sigma)=p+	r( Sigma)-2	r(\Q Sigma^{1/2}). Let  Sigma^{1/2}= oldsymbol{\Gamma} Lambda^{1/2} oldsymbol{\Gamma}\T and \G= oldsymbol{\Gamma}\T\Q oldsymbol{\Gamma}, which is orthogonal, so each \lvert g_{ii}vert\le1. Then 	r(\Q Sigma^{1/2})=	r(\G Lambda^{1/2})=\sum_ig_{ii}\lambda_i^{1/2}\le\sum_i\lambda_i^{1/2}. Since every \lambda_i>0, equality forces every g_{ii}=1. An orthogonal matrix with unit diagonal is \I, because each column has norm one. So \G=\I, which means \Q=\I. [B4] Let  Sigma=\Cov(\Y) have rank r, with spectral decomposition  Sigma= oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T, where  oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r=\I_r and  Lambda_r holds the positive eigenvalues. Show that \Z= Lambda_r^{-1/2} oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T(\Y- mu) has \Cov(\Z)=\I_r and that \Y= mu+ oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r^{1/2}\Z with probability one. Show that (\Y- mu)\T Sigma^{+}(\Y- mu)=
orm{\Z}^2, where  Sigma^+ is the Moore–Penrose inverse, and that its expectation is r. By @thm-rv-linear, \Cov(\Z)= Lambda_r^{-1/2} oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r^{-1/2}=\I_r. By @thm-rv-cov-nnd(d), \Y- mu\in\C( Sigma)=\C( oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r) with probability one, and on that event \Y- mu= oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T(\Y- mu)= oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r^{1/2}\Z. The Moore–Penrose inverse is  Sigma^+= oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r Lambda_r^{-1} oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T, so (\Y- mu)\T Sigma^+(\Y- mu)=
orm{ Lambda_r^{-1/2} oldsymbol{\Gamma}_r\T(\Y- mu)}^2=
orm{\Z}^2, with expectation 	r\Cov(\Z)=r. C. Going deeper [C1] In \Y=\X beta+ e with \X of full column rank, let \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\V with \V positive definite. Find \Cov(\hbeta) for \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y and \Cov(	ilde{ beta}) for 	ilde{ beta}=(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)^{-1}\X\T\V^{-1}\Y. Show that \Cov(\hbeta)-\Cov(	ilde{ beta}) is nonnegative definite. Hint: show that \hbeta-	ilde{ beta} and 	ilde{ beta} are uncorrelated. By @thm-rv-linear, \Cov(\hbeta)=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\V\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}, \qquad \Cov(	ilde{ beta})=\sigma^2(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)^{-1}. Write \hbeta-	ilde{ beta}= D\Y with  D=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T-(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)^{-1}\X\T\V^{-1}, and note  D\X=\I-\I= zero. Then \Cov(\hbeta-	ilde{ beta},	ilde{ beta})=\sigma^2 D\V\V^{-1}\X(\X\T\V^{-1}\X)^{-1}= zero, so by @prp-rv-sums(b), \Cov(\hbeta)=\Cov(	ilde{ beta})+\Cov(\hbeta-	ilde{ beta}), and the last term is nonnegative definite.

title: 2.3 Expectation of quadratic forms
content:
Expectation of quadratic forms Sums of squares are quadratic forms in the response. The sample variance is (n-1)^{-1}\Y\T(\I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J})\Y. The residual sum of squares of a regression is \Y\T(\I-\M)\Y, where \M is the projection onto the column space of \X (Chapter 6). Test statistics are ratios of such forms. Their expectations follow from a short trace argument that needs no distributional assumption. The basic formula [Mean of a quadratic form] Let \Y be a p	imes1 random vector with finite second moments, \E(\Y)= mu and \Cov(\Y)= Sigma, and let \A be a constant p	imes p matrix. Then \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu . A 1	imes1 matrix equals its trace, and 	r(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}\T)=\mathbf{b}\T\mathbf{a} (@thm-mat-trace-cyclic), so \Y\T\A\Y=	r(\A\Y\Y\T). By @prp-rv-expectation-linear and @prp-rv-cov-basic(b), \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r igl(\A\,\E(\Y\Y\T) igr)=	r igl(\A( Sigma+ mu mu\T) igr) =	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu . \qedhere The formula has two parts. The trace term is what the form picks up from random variation. The second term is the value of the form at the mean, which is what it would be without any randomness. The theorem does not require independence, normality or symmetry of \A. Since \Y\T\A\Y=\Y\T\A_s\Y with \A_s=	frac12(\A+\A\T), and 	r(\A Sigma)=	r(\A_s Sigma) when  Sigma is symmetric, we may assume \A symmetric whenever that is convenient. Under the conditions of @thm-rv-quadform-mean: 1. \E igl[(\Y- b)\T\A(\Y- b) igr]=	r(\A Sigma)+( mu- b)\T\A( mu- b) for any constant  b; 2. if  Sigma=\sigma^2\I, then \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\sigma^2	r(\A)+ mu\T\A mu; 3. if  Sigma is positive definite, the squared Mahalanobis distance @eq-rv-mahalanobis has \E\,\Delta^2(\Y)=p; 4. for random vectors  U (p	imes1) and \V (q	imes1) with finite second moments and a constant p	imes q matrix \A, \E( U\T\A\V)=	r igl(\A\,\Cov(\V, U) igr)+\E( U)\T\A\,\E(\V). (a) applies the theorem to \Y- b, which has covariance matrix  Sigma. (b) is immediate. (c) is (a) with  b= mu and \A= Sigma^{-1}, so the trace is 	r(\I_p)=p. For (d),  U\T\A\V=	r(\A\V U\T) and \E(\V U\T)=\Cov(\V, U)+\E(\V)\E( U)\T. [Sample variance with unequal means and variances] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be uncorrelated with means \mu_i and variances \sigma_i^2, and let S^2=(n-1)^{-1}\Y\T\mathbf{C}\Y with \mathbf{C}=\I-n^{-1}\mathbf{J}. Here  Sigma=\diag(\sigma_1^2,\dots,\sigma_n^2), so 	r(\mathbf{C} Sigma)=(1-1/n)\sum_i\sigma_i^2, and  mu\T\mathbf{C} mu=\sum_i(\mu_i- ar{\mu})^2. Therefore \E(S^2)=\overline{\sigma^2}+ rac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(\mu_i- ar{\mu})^2, \qquad \overline{\sigma^2}= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2 . With a common mean, S^2 is unbiased for the average variance, even when the variances differ. Differences in the means inflate it. That is exactly why a residual mean square estimates \sigma^2 only when the mean structure is right. [Residual sum of squares under a wrong mean] Let \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I_n and \E(\Y)= oldsymbol{	heta}, where  oldsymbol{	heta} need not lie in \C(\X). The residual sum of squares is \Y\T(\I-\M)\Y, where \M is symmetric and idempotent of rank r=ank(\X), so 	r(\I-\M)=n-r (@thm-mat-idempotent). By @cor-rv-quadform-special(b), \E(	ext{RSS})=\sigma^2(n-r)+
orm{(\I-\M) oldsymbol{	heta}}^2 . {#eq-rv-rss-mean} If the model is right,  oldsymbol{	heta}\in\C(\X), the second term vanishes and 	ext{RSS}/(n-r) is unbiased for \sigma^2. If the model is wrong, the estimate is biased upwards by the squared distance from the true mean to the model space, divided by n-r. For instance, fit a straight line at x=1,\dots,6 when the true mean is the parabola 	heta_i=	frac14(x_i-3.5)^2 and \sigma^2=1. Then \sigma^2(n-r)=4, 
orm{(\I-\M) oldsymbol{	heta}}^2=2.333, and \E(	ext{RSS})=6.333. Chapter 19 studies such departures systematically. The theorem uses only two moments, so it holds equally for skewed and heavy-tailed data. The listing checks it for a correlated vector \Y= mu+\B U, where  U has independent, centred exponential components, which are strongly skewed. With the matrices in the listing, 	r(\A Sigma)=6.9 and  mu\T\A mu=17.0, so \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=23.9. The average over 10^6 draws is 23.940, with Monte Carlo standard error 0.018. The script also verifies the formula exactly, by enumerating a discrete distribution with eight atoms. import itertools import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(20260917) mu = np.array([1.0, -1.0, 2.0]) B = np.array([[1.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.5, 1.0, 0.0], [-0.5, 0.8, 0.6]]) Sigma = B @ B.T # Cov(mu + B U) when Cov(U) = I A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0, -1.0], [0.0, -1.0, 3.0]]) theory = np.trace(A @ Sigma) + mu @ A @ mu # Theorem: no normality needed N = 1_000_000 U = rng.exponential(size=(N, 3)) - 1.0 # skewed, mean 0, variance 1 Y = mu + U @ B.T Q = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, A, Y) # Y_i' A Y_i for every draw print(f"theory {theory:.4f} simulation {Q.mean():.4f} ± {Q.std() / np.sqrt(N):.4f}") The variance needs fourth moments The mean of \Y\T\A\Y involves only \E(Y_iY_j). Its second moment involves \E(Y_iY_jY_kY_l), so no formula for \Var(\Y\T\A\Y) can be written in terms of  mu and  Sigma alone. Two random vectors with the same mean and covariance matrix can give the same quadratic form very different variances. The next theorem handles independent components, the case that matters for residual sums of squares under the classical error assumptions. Chapter 4 gives the normal case with a general  Sigma (@thm-qf-mean-var). [Variance of a quadratic form] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be independent with means 	heta_1,\dots,	heta_n and common central moments \sigma^2=\E(Y_i-	heta_i)^2, \mu_3=\E(Y_i-	heta_i)^3 and \mu_4=\E(Y_i-	heta_i)^4<\infty. Let \A be a constant symmetric n	imes n matrix, and let \mathbf{a}=(a_{11},\dots,a_{nn})\T be its diagonal. Then \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\,\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a}+2\sigma^4	r(\A^2) +4\sigma^2\, oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A^2 oldsymbol{	heta}+4\mu_3\, oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A\mathbf{a} . Write \Y= oldsymbol{	heta}+ e, where the \varepsilon_i are independent with mean zero. Then \Y\T\A\Y=q+\ell+ oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A oldsymbol{	heta},\qquad q= e\T\A e,\quad \ell=2 b\T e,\quad  b=\A oldsymbol{	heta}, so \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=\Var(q)+\Var(\ell)+2\Cov(q,\ell). We compute the three terms. The linear term. \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\I, so \Var(\ell)=4\sigma^2 b\T b=4\sigma^2 oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A^2 oldsymbol{	heta}. The cross term. Since \E(\ell)=0, \Cov(q,\ell)=\E(q\ell)=2\sum_{i,j,k}a_{ij}b_k\E(\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k). By independence and zero means, \E(\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k) vanishes unless i=j=k, when it equals \mu_3. So \Cov(q,\ell)=2\mu_3\sum_ia_{ii}b_i=2\mu_3\, oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A\mathbf{a}. The quadratic term. \E(q^2)=\sum_{i,j,k,l}a_{ij}a_{kl}\E(\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k\varepsilon_l). The fourth-order moment is \mu_4 if all four indices agree. It is \sigma^4 if the indices form two distinct pairs, which happens in three patterns: i=j
e k=l, i=k
e j=l and i=l
e j=k. Otherwise some index occurs exactly once, and the moment is zero. Using the symmetry of \A, \E(q^2)=\mu_4\sum_ia_{ii}^2+\sigma^4\Bigl[\sum_{i
e k}a_{ii}a_{kk}+2\sum_{i
e j}a_{ij}^2\Bigr] =\mu_4\,\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a}+\sigma^4 igl[(	r\A)^2-\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a}+2	r(\A^2)-2\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a} igr], since \sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=	r(\A^2). By @thm-rv-quadform-mean, \E(q)=\sigma^2	r\A, and subtracting its square gives \Var(q)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a}+2\sigma^4	r(\A^2). Adding the three terms proves the formula. For normal errors, \mu_3=0 and \mu_4=3\sigma^4, and the formula collapses to 2\sigma^4	r(\A^2)+4\sigma^2 oldsymbol{	heta}\T\A^2 oldsymbol{	heta}. Both extra terms describe how non-normality leaks into second-order behaviour. The kurtosis term depends on \A only through its diagonal. The skewness term needs both a skewed error distribution and a mean that the form does not annihilate. For the residual sum of squares of a correct model, \A oldsymbol{	heta}=(\I-\M) oldsymbol{	heta}= zero, so the skewness term disappears but the kurtosis term remains. [Skewed errors and a misspecified line] Continue @exm-rv-rss-bias, now with independent centred exponential errors, for which \sigma^2=1, \mu_3=2 and \mu_4=9. @thm-rv-quadform-variance gives \Var(	ext{RSS})=29.80. Of this, the kurtosis term contributes 16.73 and the skewness term -4.27. Normal errors with the same mean and variance would give 17.33, so the exponential errors multiply the variance by 1.72 even though the mean of RSS is unchanged. Over 10^6 simulated data sets, the variance of RSS is 30.04. The script also confirms the formula exactly for a two-point error distribution. se = Q.std() / np.sqrt(N) vals, probs = np.array([-1.0, 2.0]), np.array([2 / 3, 1 / 3]) exact = 0.0 for idx in itertools.product(range(2), repeat=3): u = vals[list(idx)] y = mu + B @ u exact += np.prod(probs[list(idx)]) * (y @ A @ y) x = np.arange(1.0, 7.0) # n = 6 design points X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x]) M = X @ np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T) A2 = np.eye(6) - M # RSS = Y'(I - M)Y for a straight line theta = 0.25 * (x - 3.5) ** 2 # true mean is curved: the line is wrong a = np.diag(A2) def var_quadform(A, theta, m2, m3, m4): """Var(Y'AY) for independent Y_i with means theta_i and common central moments.""" a = np.diag(A) return ((m4 - 3 * m2**2) * a @ a + 2 * m2**2 * np.trace(A @ A) + 4 * m2 * theta @ A @ A @ theta + 4 * m3 * theta @ A @ a) # A2 = I - M for a straight line at x = 1..6; theta = true (curved) mean mean_rss = np.trace(A2) + theta @ A2 @ theta # sigma^2 = 1 var_expo = var_quadform(A2, theta, 1.0, 2.0, 9.0) # centred exponential errors var_norm = var_quadform(A2, theta, 1.0, 0.0, 3.0) # what normal errors would give E = rng.exponential(size=(N, 6)) - 1.0 R = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", theta + E, A2, theta + E) print(f"mean {mean_rss:.3f} vs {R.mean():.3f}") print(f"var {var_expo:.3f} vs {R.var():.3f} (normal-theory value {var_norm:.3f})") Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For random vectors  U and \V of the same size, show that \E
orm{ U-\V}^2=	r\Cov( U)+	r\Cov(\V)-2	r\Cov( U,\V)+
orm{\E U-\E\V}^2. B. Practice [B1] Let \E(Y_t)=\mu and \Cov(Y_t,Y_s)=\sigma^2\phi^{\lvert t-svert} for t,s=1,\dots,n, with \lvert\phivert<1. Show that the sample variance satisfies \E(S^2)=\sigma^2\Bigl[1- rac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)\phi^k\Bigr]. Is S^2 biased up or down when \phi>0? What happens as n	o\infty with \phi fixed? With \mathbf{C}=\I-n^{-1} one one\T and \E(\Y)=\mu one, \mathbf{C}\E(\Y)= zero, so \E(\Y\T\mathbf{C}\Y)=	r(\mathbf{C} Sigma)=	r( Sigma)-n^{-1} one\T Sigma one. Here 	r( Sigma)=n\sigma^2, and  one\T Sigma one sums all entries. There are n diagonal entries and 2(n-k) entries at lag k, so  one\T Sigma one=\sigma^2 igl[n+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)\phi^k igr]. Dividing n\sigma^2-n^{-1} one\T Sigma one by n-1 gives the formula. For \phi>0 the sum is positive, so S^2 is biased downwards: positively correlated observations cluster, and the sample looks less variable than the process is. As n	o\infty the sum is O(n), so the bias is O(1/n) and vanishes. [B2] Suppose \E(\Y)=\X beta and \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\V. Show that \E(	ext{RSS})=\sigma^2	r igl((\I-\M)\V igr). For the equicorrelated \V=(1-ho)\I+ho one one\T and a model with  one\in\C(\X), show that \E(	ext{RSS})/(n-r)=\sigma^2(1-ho). [B3] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be independent and identically distributed with variance \sigma^2 and finite fourth central moment \mu_4. Use @thm-rv-quadform-variance to show that \Var(S^2)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)/n+2\sigma^4/(n-1). Compare with the normal case. Take \A=\mathbf{C}/(n-1) and  oldsymbol{	heta}=\mu one. Then \A oldsymbol{	heta}= zero, so the last two terms of @thm-rv-quadform-variance vanish. Every diagonal entry of \A is (1-1/n)/(n-1)=1/n, so \mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{a}=1/n, and 	r(\A^2)=	r(\mathbf{C})/(n-1)^2=1/(n-1). This gives the formula. Normal data have \mu_4=3\sigma^4 and \Var(S^2)=2\sigma^4/(n-1). Heavy tails (\mu_4>3\sigma^4) add a term of the same order 1/n, so the normal-theory variance is wrong even in large samples. [B4] Under the conditions of @thm-rv-quadform-variance with  oldsymbol{	heta}= zero, show that \Cov(\Y\T\A\Y,\Y\T\B\Y)=(\mu_4-3\sigma^4)\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{b}+2\sigma^4	r(\A\B), where \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} are the diagonals of the symmetric matrices \A and \B. Hint: apply the theorem to \A+\B. [B5] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n be independent \Normal(0,\sigma^2). Among symmetric \A with \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\sigma^2, show that \Var(\Y\T\A\Y) is minimized by \A=n^{-1}\I. Hint: 	r(\A^2)\ge(	r\A)^2/n.

title: 2.4 Correlation matrices
content: Correlation matrices Covariances carry units: the covariance of income in dollars with age in years is in dollar-years. To compare the strength of linear association across pairs of variables, each covariance is divided by the two standard deviations. [Correlation matrix] Let \Y have covariance matrix \bSigma=(\sigma_{ij}) with every \sigma_{ii}>0, and let \bD_\sigma=\diag(\sigma_{11}^{1/2},\dots,\sigma_{pp}^{1/2}) be the diagonal matrix of standard deviations. The correlation matrix of \Y is \R=\bD_\sigma^{-1}\bSigma\bD_\sigma^{-1}, \qquad\text{with entries}\qquad \rho_{ij}=\frac{\sigma_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{jj}}}=\operatorname{corr}(Y_i,Y_j). Equivalently \bSigma=\bD_\sigma\R\bD_\sigma. For random vectors \bU and \V with standard-deviation matrices \bD_U and \bD_V, the cross-correlation matrix is \bD_U^{-1}\Cov(\bU,\V)\bD_V^{-1}. Some books write \mathbf{P}_\rho for the correlation matrix. We use \R in this chapter, and \hat{\R} for its sample counterpart in Section 2.7. [Properties of correlation matrices] Let \R be the correlation matrix of \Y. 1. \R is the covariance matrix of the standardized vector \Z=\bD_\sigma^{-1}(\Y-\bmu). Hence \R is nonnegative definite with unit diagonal, and \tr(\R)=p. 2. \lvert\rho_{ij}\rvert\le1, with \lvert\rho_{ij}\rvert=1 iff Z_j=\rho_{ij}Z_i with probability one. 3. \rank(\R)=\rank(\bSigma). In particular, \R is positive definite iff \bSigma is. 4. If \Y^*=\bD\Y+\mathbf{c} with \bD=\diag(d_1,\dots,d_p) and every d_i\ne0, then \rho^*_{ij}=\operatorname{sign}(d_id_j)\,\rho_{ij}. Positive rescaling and shifting leave \R unchanged. 5. Conversely, every nonnegative definite matrix with unit diagonal is the correlation matrix of some random vector. (a) @thm-rv-linear gives \Cov(\Z)=\bD_\sigma^{-1}\bSigma\bD_\sigma^{-1}=\R, and @thm-rv-cov-nnd(a) applies. (b) The 2\times2 matrix of rows and columns i,j of \R is the covariance matrix of (Z_i,Z_j), so it is nonnegative definite and its determinant 1-\rho_{ij}^2 is nonnegative. If \rho_{ij}=\pm1, the vector (\rho_{ij},-1)\T is in the null space of that 2\times2 matrix, so \rho_{ij}Z_i-Z_j=0 with probability one by @thm-rv-cov-nnd(c). Conversely, Z_j=cZ_i with \Var(Z_i)=\Var(Z_j)=1 forces c=\pm1 and \rho_{ij}=c. (c) \bD_\sigma is nonsingular. (d) \Cov(\Y^*)=\bD\bSigma\bD has entries d_id_j\sigma_{ij} and standard deviations \lvert d_i\rvert\sigma_{ii}^{1/2}. (e) Such a matrix is a covariance matrix by @thm-rv-cov-nnd(b), and its variances are one. Part (d) is the reason correlation is the natural scale-free summary. Part (e) is less obvious than it looks. A symmetric matrix with unit diagonal and off-diagonal entries in [-1,1] need not be a correlation matrix, because the correlations must be jointly consistent. [Three correlations] Let \lvert\rho_{12}\rvert<1 and \lvert\rho_{13}\rvert<1. The matrix \R=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho_{12}&\rho_{13}\\\rho_{12}&1&\rho_{23}\\\rho_{13}&\rho_{23}&1\end{pmatrix} is a correlation matrix iff \rho_{12}\rho_{13}-\sqrt{(1-\rho_{12}^2)(1-\rho_{13}^2)} \;\le\;\rho_{23}\;\le\; \rho_{12}\rho_{13}+\sqrt{(1-\rho_{12}^2)(1-\rho_{13}^2)} . By @prp-rv-correlation(e) we must decide when \R is nonnegative definite. Write \mathbf{r}=(\rho_{12},\rho_{13})\T and let \R_2 be the lower right 2\times2 block. The nonsingular matrix \bT=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&\bzero\T\\-\mathbf{r}&\I_2\end{psmallmatrix} gives \bT\R\bT\T=\begin{pmatrix}1&\bzero\T\\\bzero&\R_2-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}\T\end{pmatrix}, and \mathbf{a}\T\R\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}\T(\bT\R\bT\T)\mathbf{b} with \mathbf{b}=(\bT\T)^{-1}\mathbf{a} ranges over all vectors as \mathbf{a} does. So \R is nonnegative definite iff the Schur complement \R_2-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}\T=\begin{pmatrix}1-\rho_{12}^2&\rho_{23}-\rho_{12}\rho_{13}\\ \rho_{23}-\rho_{12}\rho_{13}&1-\rho_{13}^2\end{pmatrix} is. A symmetric 2\times2 matrix with positive diagonal is nonnegative definite iff its determinant is nonnegative, because its eigenvalues have positive sum and their product is the determinant. The determinant is (1-\rho_{12}^2)(1-\rho_{13}^2)-(\rho_{23}-\rho_{12}\rho_{13})^2, and it is nonnegative exactly on the stated interval. If Y_2 and Y_3 both correlate 0.8 with Y_1, the interval is [0.28,1]. Two variables that are strongly related to a third cannot be negatively correlated with each other, nor even uncorrelated. The quantity (\rho_{23}-\rho_{12}\rho_{13})/\sqrt{(1-\rho_{12}^2)(1-\rho_{13}^2)}, which the proof forces into [-1,1], is the correlation of Y_2 and Y_3 after the linear effect of Y_1 has been removed from both.
