By @cor-ci-shadows, the values of \mathbf{a}\T oldsymbol{\phi}_0 over the ellipse fill the interval \mathbf{a}\T\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}\pm\sqrt{2F_\alpha}\,s\sqrt{\mathbf{a}\T\W\mathbf{a}}, so the line meets the ellipse iff this interval contains 0. The t test uses the smaller multiplier t_{n-r,\alpha/2}. It is the right test for a hypothesis fixed in advance. The ellipse criterion is the right one for a contrast chosen after looking at the estimates, because it holds simultaneously for all \mathbf{a}. [B3] Let the columns of  Lambda lie in \C(\X\T) but be linearly dependent, with ank( Lambda)=k<q. Show that \W= Lambda\T\G Lambda is singular, that \hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}- oldsymbol{\phi}\in\C(\W) with probability one, and that  egin{aligned}  igl\{ oldsymbol{\phi}_0\in\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}+\C(\W):\ &(\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}- oldsymbol{\phi}_0)\T\W\ginv(\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}- oldsymbol{\phi}_0)\ &\le k\,s^2F_\alpha(k,n-r) igr\} \end{aligned} is an exact 1-\alpha confidence set, a k-dimensional ellipsoid inside a k-dimensional affine subspace of \Real^q. \W=(\M T)\T(\M T) has rank ank(\M T)=ank( Lambda)=k (proof of @cor-opt-quadratic). The vector \hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}- oldsymbol{\phi} is \Normal_q( zero,\sigma^2\W), so it lies in \C(\W) almost surely (@thm-rv-cov-nnd). By @cor-opt-quadratic the quadratic form over k\,s^2 is F(k,n-r) and does not depend on the generalized inverse. So the displayed set covers  oldsymbol{\phi} with probability 1-\alpha. Restricted to the affine subspace, write \W=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}\T with \mathbf{U} (q	imes k) orthonormal and \mathbf{D} positive diagonal. For  oldsymbol{\phi}_0-\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{c}, the form is \mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{c}, an ellipsoid in the coordinates \mathbf{c}. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \X have full column rank. Show that the confidence ellipsoid for  beta is a region of the form \{ b:\ \ell_p( b)\ge\ell_p(\hbeta)-k\}, where \ell_p( b)=\max_{\sigma^2}\ell( b,\sigma^2) is the profile log-likelihood of Chapter 7, and find k in terms of F_\alpha(p,n-p). How does k compare with the value 	frac12\chi^2_\alpha(p) suggested by the asymptotic theory of likelihood ratios? The profile log-likelihood is \ell_p( b)=	ext{const}-	frac n2\log
orm{\Y-\X b}^2, and 
orm{\Y-\X b}^2=	ext{SSE}+(\hbeta- b)\T\X\T\X(\hbeta- b) by @eq-proj-distance-split. So \ell_p(\hbeta)-\ell_p( b)=	frac n2\log\{1+pF_{ b}/(n-p)\}, where F_{ b} is the statistic of @thm-ci-ellipsoid(c). This is increasing in F_{ b}, so the ellipsoid is the region with k=	frac n2\log\{1+pF_\alpha(p,n-p)/(n-p)\}. As n	o\infty, pF_\alpha(p,n-p)	o\chi^2_\alpha(p) and k	o	frac12\chi^2_\alpha(p). For finite n, k is larger, and the exact region is larger than the asymptotic likelihood region.

title: 12.3 Prediction intervals
content:
Prediction intervals Often the quantity of interest is an observation not yet made: tomorrow’s stack loss, or the reading of the next specimen. An interval for it must allow for the error in the estimated mean, which shrinks as data accumulate, and the error of the new observation itself, which does not. The first depends on where the new point lies relative to the data; the second makes prediction intervals depend on normality in a way that confidence intervals do not. Predicting a new observation Let the data follow the normal linear model of Section 12.1, and let Y_0=\x_0\T beta+\varepsilon_0,\qquad \varepsilon_0\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2),\ \ \varepsilon_0	ext{ independent of }\Y, {#eq-ci-new-observation} be a future observation at a regressor vector \x_0\in\C(\X\T). The requirement \x_0\in\C(\X\T) makes the mean \x_0\T beta estimable. Without it, @prp-ci-nonestimable shows that nothing useful can be said. We call h_0=\x_0\T\G\x_0 the leverage of the new point. When \x_0 is the ith row of \X, h_0 is the diagonal entry h_{ii} of \M (@prp-proj-leverage), and \sigma^2h_0 is always the variance of \hat{Y}_0=\x_0\T\hbeta (@thm-opt-sampling(a)). [Prediction interval] Under @eq-ci-new-observation, put \hat{Y}_0=\x_0\T\hbeta. 1. Y_0-\hat{Y}_0\sim\Normal igl(0,\sigma^2(1+h_0) igr), it is independent of s^2, and  rac{Y_0-\hat{Y}_0}{s\sqrt{1+h_0}}\sim t(n-r). 2. The interval \hat{Y}_0\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_0} contains Y_0 with probability exactly 1-\alpha, the probability being computed over \Y and Y_0 jointly, at every ( beta,\sigma^2). 3. More generally, if  ar{Y}_0 is the mean of m independent new observations at \x_0, each distributed as in @eq-ci-new-observation, then \hat{Y}_0\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1/m+h_0} contains  ar{Y}_0 with probability exactly 1-\alpha. As m	o\infty this interval becomes the confidence interval \hat{Y}_0\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{h_0} for \x_0\T beta. We prove (c), of which (a) and (b) are the case m=1. The new observations are independent of \Y, and  ar{Y}_0\sim\Normal(\x_0\T beta,\sigma^2/m). The vector ( ar{Y}_0,\Y\T)\T is normal with independent blocks, so  ar{Y}_0-\hat{Y}_0, a linear function of it, is normal (@thm-mvn-linear) with mean \x_0\T beta-\x_0\T beta=0 and variance \sigma^2/m+\sigma^2h_0, the two terms adding because  ar{Y}_0 and \hat{Y}_0 are independent. For independence from s^2: \hat{Y}_0 is a function of \M\Y, and \M\Y and SSE are independent (@thm-opt-sampling(c)). Since  ar{Y}_0 is independent of \Y, for any events,  egin{aligned} &\Pr( ar{Y}_0\in A,\ \M\Y\in B,\ 	ext{SSE}\in D)\ &\qquad=\Pr( ar{Y}_0\in A)\Pr(\M\Y\in B)\Pr(	ext{SSE}\in D), \end{aligned} so ( ar{Y}_0,\M\Y) is independent of SSE, and so is  ar{Y}_0-\hat{Y}_0. Dividing the standardized normal variable by \sqrt{(	ext{SSE}/\sigma^2)/(n-r)} gives t(n-r) (@def-qf-noncentral-t), and the interval statement is \Pr\{\lvert Tvert\le t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\}=1-\alpha. The limit as m	o\infty is immediate, and the limiting interval is @eq-ci-t-interval with  lambda=\x_0. Part (a) was sketched in @exr-opt-prediction-t. A prediction interval is for a random variable, and its probability refers to the joint experiment: collect the data, compute the interval, observe Y_0. Given the data, the probability that the interval contains Y_0 is random,  egin{aligned} \Pr igl(Y_0\in	ext{interval}\mid\Y igr)&=\Phi\Bigl( rac{\x_0\T(\hbeta- beta)+t\,s\sqrt{1+h_0}}{\sigma}\Bigr)\ &\quad-\Phi\Bigl( rac{\x_0\T(\hbeta- beta)-t\,s\sqrt{1+h_0}}{\sigma}\Bigr), \end{aligned} with t=t_{n-r,\alpha/2} and \Phi the standard normal distribution function, and it is only its expectation that equals 1-\alpha. In the variance \sigma^2(1+h_0), the leverage h_0 is the price of not knowing  beta, of order r/n at a typical point (@prp-proj-leverage). The 1 is the new error, which no amount of data removes: the prediction interval never becomes shorter than about 2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma, while the interval for the mean shrinks to a point. [Predicting a state’s murder rate] In the murder-rate regression, consider a state at the centroid of the regressors. Its leverage is h_0=1/n=0.0200 (see @prp-ci-new-leverage), the fitted rate is 4.514, and the 95\% intervals are 	ext{mean response: }(4.090,\ 4.938),\qquad 	ext{new state: }(1.487,\ 7.541). The prediction interval is 7.14 times as long as the interval for the mean, and nearly all of its length, 6.053 per 100,000, comes from s. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import stats data = sm.datasets.statecrime.load_pandas().data data = data.drop(index="District of Columbia") y = data["murder"].to_numpy() X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), data[["poverty", "single", "urban"]]]) n, p = X.shape C = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) beta_hat = C @ X.T @ y s = np.sqrt(np.sum((y - X @ beta_hat) ** 2) / (n - p)) q = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - p) h = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", X, C, X) # leverages of the 50 states def intervals(x0): """Leverage h0, 95% interval for the mean response, 95% prediction interval.""" h0 = x0 @ C @ x0 fit = x0 @ beta_hat ci = (fit - q * s * np.sqrt(h0), fit + q * s * np.sqrt(h0)) pi = (fit - q * s * np.sqrt(1 + h0), fit + q * s * np.sqrt(1 + h0)) return h0, fit, ci, pi x_centre = X.mean(axis=0) # the average state x_hidden = np.array([1.0, 20.0, 19.0, 60.0]) # each coordinate inside its observed range for name, x0 in [("centre", x_centre), ("hidden", x_hidden)]: h0, fit, ci, pi = intervals(x0) print(f"{name}: h0 = {h0:.4f}, fit {fit:.3f}, mean ({ci[0]:.3f}, {ci[1]:.3f}), " f"new state ({pi[0]:.3f}, {pi[1]:.3f})") print(f"largest leverage in the data: {h.max():.4f}") Leverage and extrapolation [Leverage of a new point] Let \x_0=\X\T oldsymbol{ho}\in\C(\X\T) and h_0=\x_0\T\G\x_0. 1. h_0=\min\{
orm{\mathbf{a}}^2:\ \X\T\mathbf{a}=\x_0\}, and the minimum is attained only at \mathbf{a}=\M oldsymbol{ho}. 2. If \X=[ one,\X_1] has full column rank, \x_0=(1,\x_{01}\T)\T,  ar{\x} is the vector of column means of \X_1 and 	ilde{\X}_1=\X_1- one ar{\x}\T, then h_0= rac1n+(\x_{01}- ar{\x})\T igl(	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1 igr)^{-1}(\x_{01}- ar{\x}). 3. If further columns are added, \X_+=[\X,\mathbf{Z}], and \x_{0+}=(\x_0\T,\mathbf{z}_0\T)\T\in\C(\X_+\T), then the leverage of \x_{0+} in the enlarged model is at least h_0. (a) Let \X\T\mathbf{a}=\x_0. Then \X\T\M\mathbf{a}=\X\T\mathbf{a}=\x_0=\X\T\M oldsymbol{ho}, so \M\mathbf{a}-\M oldsymbol{ho} lies in \C(\X) and is orthogonal to \C(\X); hence \M\mathbf{a}=\M oldsymbol{ho}. By Pythagoras, 
orm{\mathbf{a}}^2=
orm{\M oldsymbol{ho}}^2+
orm{(\I-\M)\mathbf{a}}^2\ge
orm{\M oldsymbol{ho}}^2, with equality iff \mathbf{a}=\M oldsymbol{ho}, and 
orm{\M oldsymbol{ho}}^2= oldsymbol{ho}\T\X\G\X\T oldsymbol{ho}=h_0 by @thm-proj-M-formula. (b) \X=[ one,	ilde{\X}_1]\A with \A= egin{pmatrix}1& ar{\x}\T\ zero&\I\end{pmatrix}, which is invertible. Since  one\T	ilde{\X}_1= zero\T, \X\T\X=\A\T\diag igl(n,	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1 igr)\A, and so h_0= w\T\diag igl(1/n,(	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1)^{-1} igr) w with  w=\A^{-	op}\x_0. Solving \A\T w=\x_0 gives  w=(1,(\x_{01}- ar{\x})\T)\T. (c) Every \mathbf{a} with \X_+\T\mathbf{a}=\x_{0+} also satisfies \X\T\mathbf{a}=\x_0. A minimum over a smaller set is at least as large, so (a), applied to both models, gives the claim. Part (a) is the Gauss–Markov theorem in disguise. Part (b) makes leverage a distance: the quadratic form is (n-1)^{-1} times the squared Mahalanobis distance of \x_{01} from the centroid of the regressors, as for the observed points (@prp-proj-leverage-mahalanobis). So the interval for the mean is shortest at the centroid, where h_0=1/n, and widens along ellipsoidal contours. Part (c) says a larger model never predicts more precisely at a given point, though it may predict with less bias; Chapter 29 weighs the two. With several correlated regressors, a point can lie inside the range of every regressor and still be far from the data, because it breaks their correlation. This hidden extrapolation is detected by the leverage, not by the separate ranges. [Hidden extrapolation] Poverty ranges from 8.5\% to 21.9\% over the 50 states, and single-parent households from 17.9\% to 32.8\%. A state with poverty 20\%, single-parent households 19\% and 60\% urban is inside every range, but poor with few single parents, a combination absent from the data. Its leverage is h_0=0.435, far above the largest leverage among the actual states, 0.260 (Mississippi). Figure 12.3.1 shows the contours of h_0 over the two regressors, with urbanization held at its mean. The fitted rate is 3.817. The 95\% interval for the mean is (1.840,\ 5.794), longer than at the centroid by the factor \sqrt{0.435/0.0200}=4.66. The prediction interval, (0.227,\ 7.407), is only 1.186 times as long as at the centroid, because it is dominated by s. The prediction interval barely registers the extrapolation, and the real danger, that the model may be wrong where there are no data to check it, is in neither formula. If urbanization is dropped from the model the leverage of this point falls to 0.287, as @prp-ci-new-leverage(c) requires. [Figure 12.3.1. Contours of the leverage h_0 of a new state (urbanization at its mean), with the 50 states, the box of observed ranges (dotted) and the largest observed leverage (dashed). The marked state is inside the box but far from the data.] Figure 12.3.1. Contours of the leverage h_0 of a new state (urbanization at its mean), with the 50 states, the box of observed ranges (dotted) and the largest observed leverage (dashed). The marked state is inside the box but far from the data. [Contours of the leverage h_0 of a new state (urbanization at its mean), with the 50 states, the box of observed ranges (dotted) and the largest observed leverage (dashed). The marked state is inside the box but far from the data.] Contours of the leverage h_0 of a new state (urbanization at its mean), with the 50 states, the box of observed ranges (dotted) and the largest observed leverage (dashed). The marked state is inside the box but far from the data. When the errors are not normal The estimate \hat{Y}_0 is a weighted sum of n errors, approximately normal by a central limit theorem when no weight dominates (Chapter 19). The new error \varepsilon_0 is a single draw, and its distribution enters the prediction interval unchanged, however large n is. [Prediction intervals without normality] Consider a sequence of full-rank models \Y_n=\X_n beta+ e_n with p fixed and n	o\infty, and a fixed \x_0 whose leverage h_{0,n}=\x_0\T(\X_n\T\X_n)^{-1}\x_0 tends to zero. Let \varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n and \varepsilon_0 be independent and identically distributed with mean 0, variance \sigma^2, finite fourth moment and a continuous distribution function, and let Y_0=\x_0\T beta+\varepsilon_0. Then the coverage of the nominal 1-\alpha prediction interval \hat{Y}_0\pm t_{n-p,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_{0,n}} satisfies  egin{aligned} &\Pr igl\{\lvert Y_0-\hat{Y}_0vert\le t_{n-p,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_{0,n}} igr\}\ &\qquad\longrightarrow\ \Pr igl\{\lvert\varepsilon_0vert\le z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma igr\}, \end{aligned} where z_{\alpha/2} is the upper \alpha/2 point of \Normal(0,1). Likewise the probabilities of missing above and below tend to \Pr\{\varepsilon_0>z_{\alpha/2}\sigma\} and \Pr\{\varepsilon_0<-z_{\alpha/2}\sigma\}. Write T_n=(Y_0-\hat{Y}_0)/(s\sqrt{1+h_{0,n}}), t_n=t_{n-p,\alpha/2} and E=\varepsilon_0/\sigma. First, Y_0-\hat{Y}_0=\varepsilon_0-\x_0\T(\hbeta- beta), and \x_0\T(\hbeta- beta) has mean zero and variance \sigma^2h_{0,n}	o0 (@thm-lm-moments), so it tends to zero in probability by Chebyshev’s inequality. Second, s	o\sigma in probability (@cor-lm-s2-consistent), and t_n	o z_{\alpha/2}. Hence D_n=T_n-E	o0 in probability. Fix \eta>0. On the event \{\lvert D_nvert\le\eta/2,\ \lvert t_n-z_{\alpha/2}vert\le\eta/2\}, whose probability tends to one, \lvert Evert\le z_{\alpha/2}-\eta\ \Longrightarrow\ \lvert T_nvert\le t_n\ \Longrightarrow\ \lvert Evert\le z_{\alpha/2}+\eta . So \Pr\{\lvert Evert\le z_{\alpha/2}-\eta\}\le\liminf\Pr\{\lvert T_nvert\le t_n\}\le\limsup\Pr\{\lvert T_nvert\le t_n\}\le\Pr\{\lvert Evert\le z_{\alpha/2}+\eta\}. The distribution function of E is continuous, so letting \eta	o0 gives the limit. The one-sided statements are proved the same way. The limit is the nominal 1-\alpha only if \Pr\{\lvert\varepsilon_0vert\le z_{\alpha/2}\sigma\}=1-\alpha, a property of the normal distribution, not of large samples. A simulation shows both effects: a straight line with n equally spaced design points on [0,1], prediction at x_0=0.8, and errors with mean zero and variance one that are normal, centred exponential (skewed) or uniform (short-tailed). With 20000 data sets for each case, the coverages of the nominal 80\% and 95\% intervals are: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Errors n mean, 80% mean, 95% new obs., 80% new obs., 95% ------------- ----------- ----------- ----------- --------------- --------------- normal 20 0.799 0.949 0.797 0.949 normal 400 0.805 0.953 0.802 0.953 exponential 20 0.774 0.931 0.863 0.939 exponential 400 0.799 0.949 0.896 0.949 uniform 20 0.797 0.948 0.787 0.983 uniform 400 0.800 0.950 0.741 1.000 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- At n=400 the intervals for the mean are near nominal for every law, while the prediction intervals approach the limits of @prp-ci-pi-limit: 0.898 and 0.948 (exponential), 0.740 and 1.000 (uniform). The exponential 95\% interval looks fine only by accident: at n=400 it misses above in a proportion 0.051 of the samples and below in 0.0000, since a centred exponential error is never below -1. rng = np.random.default_rng(1203) laws = { "normal": lambda size: rng.normal(size=size), "exponential": lambda size: rng.exponential(size=size) - 1.0, # skewed "uniform": lambda size: rng.uniform(-np.sqrt(3), np.sqrt(3), size=size), # short tails } # all: mean 0, variance 1 x0_sim = 0.8 def simulate(law, n_sim, reps=20_000): x = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_sim) Xs = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_sim), x]) Hs = np.linalg.solve(Xs.T @ Xs, Xs.T) # beta_hat = Hs y z0 = np.array([1.0, x0_sim]) h0 = z0 @ np.linalg.solve(Xs.T @ Xs, z0) E = laws[law]((reps, n_sim)) # true beta = 0, sigma = 1 fit = E @ (Hs.T @ z0) s_sim = np.sqrt(np.sum((E - (E @ Hs.T) @ Xs.T) ** 2, axis=1) / (n_sim - 2)) new = laws[law](reps) # the new observation's error out = {} for level in (0.80, 0.95): t = stats.t.ppf(0.5 + level / 2, n_sim - 2) out[("mean", level)] = np.mean(np.abs(fit) <= t * s_sim * np.sqrt(h0)) out[("new", level)] = np.mean(np.abs(new - fit) <= t * s_sim * np.sqrt(1 + h0)) return out table = {(law, m): simulate(law, m) for law in laws for m in (20, 400)} for (law, m), out in table.items(): print(f"{law:12s} n = {m:3d}: " + ", ".join(f"{k[0]} {k[1]:.2f}: {v:.3f}" for k, v in out.items())) Remedies, transformation (Chapter 22) and resampling (Chapter 23), come later. Checking normality matters much more for prediction than for estimation. [Prediction is not intervention] A prediction interval describes the next observation from the same process. If the regressors are set by intervention, say a policy that changes a state’s poverty rate, the observed association need not describe what happens (Chapter 25). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Show that the ratio of the length of the prediction interval to that of the confidence interval for the mean at \x_0 is \sqrt{(1+h_0)/h_0}. What is it in @exm-ci-state-prediction, and what happens to it as n	o\infty with the design growing regularly? Both intervals use the multiplier t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s, with \sqrt{1+h_0} and \sqrt{h_0} respectively. At the centroid, h_0=0.0200 and the ratio is \sqrt{51}=7.14. As the design grows, h_0	o0 and the ratio tends to infinity: the confidence interval shrinks to a point while the prediction interval does not. B. Practice [B1] Two new observations will be made, at \x_{01} and \x_{02}, with independent errors. Find an exact 1-\alpha prediction interval for their difference Y_{01}-Y_{02}. Show that when \x_{01}=\x_{02} it does not depend on the data except through s. Y_{01}-Y_{02}-(\x_{01}-\x_{02})\T\hbeta is normal with mean zero and variance \sigma^2\{2+(\x_{01}-\x_{02})\T\G(\x_{01}-\x_{02})\}, independent of s^2 by the argument of @thm-ci-prediction-interval. The interval is (\x_{01}-\x_{02})\T\hbeta\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{2+(\x_{01}-\x_{02})\T\G(\x_{01}-\x_{02})}. When the two points coincide it is \pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt2: the difference of two new errors, for which the fitted model contributes only its estimate of \sigma. [B2] In @prp-ci-new-leverage(c), let \X have full column rank and add a single column  z
otin\C(\X). Show that the new leverage is h_{0+}=h_0+ rac{(z_0-\mathbf{k}\T\x_0)^2}{
orm{(\I-\M) z}^2},\qquad \mathbf{k}=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T z . So the leverage is unchanged iff z_0 equals the value \mathbf{k}\T\x_0 predicted for it by the other regressors. Use @prp-ci-new-leverage(a) for the enlarged model. Write \x_0=\X\T oldsymbol{ho} and split any feasible \mathbf{a} as \mathbf{a}=\M\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} with \mathbf{b}\perp\C(\X). The constraint \X\T\mathbf{a}=\x_0 forces \M\mathbf{a}=\M oldsymbol{ho}, as in the proof of the proposition. The constraint  z\T\mathbf{a}=z_0 then reads  z\T\M oldsymbol{ho}+ z\T\mathbf{b}=z_0, and  z\T\M oldsymbol{ho}= z\T\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T oldsymbol{ho}=\mathbf{k}\T\x_0. Since \mathbf{b}\perp\C(\X),  z\T\mathbf{b}=((\I-\M) z)\T\mathbf{b}, and by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality the shortest \mathbf{b} with ((\I-\M) z)\T\mathbf{b}=z_0-\mathbf{k}\T\x_0 is a multiple of (\I-\M) z, with 
orm{\mathbf{b}}^2=(z_0-\mathbf{k}\T\x_0)^2/
orm{(\I-\M) z}^2. Adding 
orm{\M oldsymbol{ho}}^2=h_0 gives the formula. [B3] For the line through the origin, \E Y_i= eta x_i with \sum x_i^2>0, write the 1-\alpha confidence interval for the mean at x_0 and the prediction interval for Y_0. Show that the confidence interval for the mean has length proportional to \lvert x_0vert, and is a point at x_0=0. Why is that reasonable, and what does it assume? Here r=1, \hat{ eta}=\sum x_iy_i/\sum x_i^2, s^2=\sum(y_i-\hat{ eta} x_i)^2/(n-1) and h_0=x_0^2/\sum x_i^2. The intervals are \hat{ eta} x_0\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\,s\lvert x_0vert/\sqrt{\sum x_i^2} and \hat{ eta} x_0\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+x_0^2/\sum x_i^2}. At x_0=0 the model asserts that the mean is exactly zero, so there is nothing to estimate. The interval is only as good as that assertion: if the true line has a small intercept, the interval near x_0=0 is too short. [B4] Suppose the new regressor vector \mathbf{X}_0 is random, independent of the pair (\Y,\varepsilon_0), and always lies in \C(\X\T). Show that the prediction interval of @thm-ci-prediction-interval, computed at the realized \mathbf{X}_0, still covers Y_0 with probability exactly 1-\alpha. Condition on \mathbf{X}_0=\x_0. By independence, given this event (\Y,\varepsilon_0) has its unconditional distribution, so @thm-ci-prediction-interval applies and the conditional coverage is 1-\alpha for every \x_0. Averaging over the distribution of \mathbf{X}_0 gives 1-\alpha. C. Going deeper [C1] Let k new observations be made at the rows of a k	imes p matrix \X_0 whose rows lie in \C(\X\T), with errors independent of each other and of \Y. Show that \mathbf{D}=\mathbf{Y}_0-\X_0\hbeta\sim\Normal_k igl( zero,\sigma^2(\I_k+\X_0\G\X_0\T) igr), independent of s^2, and deduce that the intervals \x_{0j}\T\hbeta\ \pm\ \sqrt{k\,F_\alpha(k,n-r)}\ s\sqrt{1+h_{0j}},\qquad j=1,\dots,k, contain all k new observations simultaneously with probability at least 1-\alpha. Normality, the mean and the covariance follow as in @thm-ci-prediction-interval, and \mathbf{S}=\I_k+\X_0\G\X_0\T is positive definite. So \mathbf{D}\T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{D}/(k s^2)\sim F(k,n-r) (@cor-qf-mahalanobis and @def-qf-noncentral-f). By @lem-ci-cauchy-schwarz with \mathbf{a}=\vect{e}_j, the event \mathbf{D}\T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{D}\le k s^2F_\alpha implies \lvert D_jvert\le\sqrt{kF_\alpha}\,s\sqrt{S_{jj}} for every j, and S_{jj}=1+h_{0j}. Chapter 13 compares this with Bonferroni’s method, which is shorter when k is small. [C2] A (P,1-\alpha) tolerance interval at \x_0 is a random interval that, with probability at least 1-\alpha over \Y, contains at least a proportion P of the distribution of Y_0. Show that the prediction interval of @thm-ci-prediction-interval is not a (1-\alpha,1-\alpha) tolerance interval, by showing that its conditional coverage given \Y is below 1-\alpha with probability bounded away from zero. Construct a conservative tolerance interval from a lower confidence bound for the conditional coverage, using a 1-\alpha/2 upper confidence bound for \sigma and a 1-\alpha/2 confidence interval for \x_0\T beta.

title: 12.4 Simultaneous bands for the regression line and surface
content:
Simultaneous bands for the regression line and surface A fitted line is usually drawn inside a shaded region. If the region is made of pointwise intervals, each vertical slice covers the true mean with probability 1-\alpha, but the region does not cover the whole true line with that probability. A reader who asks “which lines are consistent with the data?” needs a simultaneous band, and for a linear model the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives one with exact coverage. Pointwise is not simultaneous [Simultaneous confidence band] Let \mathcal S\subseteq\C(\X\T) be a set of regressor vectors. Random functions \ell(\x)=\ell(\x;\Y) and u(\x)=u(\x;\Y) form a 1-\alpha simultaneous confidence band for the regression function over \mathcal S if \Pr_{ beta,\sigma^2} igl\{\ell(\x)\le\x\T beta\le u(\x)\ 	ext{ for every }\x\in\mathcal S igr\}\ \ge\ 1-\alpha for every ( beta,\sigma^2). Pointwise t intervals fail this: for the stack loss line of @exm-ci-stackloss-band, the pointwise 95\% intervals cover the true line over the observed range in only 0.8705 of simulated samples. The Working–Hotelling band [Working–Hotelling band] Let \mathcal L be a linear subspace of \C(\X\T) of dimension k\ge1, and let w_k=\sqrt{k\,F_\alpha(k,n-r)}. Then \Pr igl\{\lvert\x\T\hbeta-\x\T betavert\le w_k\,s\sqrt{\x\T\G\x}\ 	ext{ for all }\x\in\mathcal L igr\}=1-\alpha . {#eq-ci-wh-band} In particular: 1. with \mathcal L=\C(\X\T) and k=r, the functions \x\T\hbeta\pm w_r\,s\sqrt{\x\T\G\x} form an exact 1-\alpha simultaneous band for the regression surface over all estimable \x; 2. for a straight line \E Y_i= eta_0+ eta_1x_i with the x_i not all equal, the band \hat{ eta}_0+\hat{ eta}_1x\ \pm\ \sqrt{2F_\alpha(2,n-2)}\ s\,\sqrt{ rac1n+ rac{(x- ar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}},\qquad x\in\Real, contains the true line  eta_0+ eta_1x for every real x with probability exactly 1-\alpha. Step 1: from \mathcal L to a subspace of \C(\X). The map  u\mapsto\X\T u is one to one on \C(\X), since \X\T u= zero with  u\in\C(\X) forces  u\in\C(\X)\cap\C(\X)\perpc=\{ zero\}. It maps \C(\X) onto \C(\X\T), because \X\T oldsymbol{ho}=\X\T\M oldsymbol{ho}. So \mathcal U=\{ u\in\C(\X):\X\T u\in\mathcal L\} is a subspace of \C(\X) of dimension k, and every \x\in\mathcal L is \X\T u for exactly one  u\in\mathcal U. For such a pair,  egin{aligned} \x\T\hbeta-\x\T beta&= u\T(\X\hbeta-\X beta)= u\T\M(\Y-\X beta)= u\T v,\ \x\T\G\x&= u\T\X\G\X\T u= u\T\M u=
orm u^2, \end{aligned} where  v= P_{\mathcal U}(\Y-\X beta). The middle equality uses \X\hbeta=\M\Y and \M\X=\X. The last step of the first chain uses  u=\M u= P_{\mathcal U} u, and the second chain uses @thm-proj-M-formula. Step 2: the supremum. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, for  u\in\mathcal U,  u
e zero,  rac{(\x\T\hbeta-\x\T beta)^2}{\x\T\G\x}= rac{( u\T v)^2}{
orm u^2}\le
orm v^2, with equality at  u= v when  v
e zero, and  v\in\mathcal U. So the supremum of the left side over \x\in\mathcal L\setminus\{ zero\} equals 
orm v^2 and is attained. Step 3: its distribution. \Y-\X beta\sim\Normal_n( zero,\sigma^2\I), and  P_{\mathcal U} is symmetric idempotent of rank k, so 
orm v^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(k) (@thm-qf-chisq(a)). Since \mathcal U\subseteq\C(\X),  P_{\mathcal U}= P_{\mathcal U}\M, so  v is a function of \M\Y and is independent of SSE (@thm-opt-sampling(c)). Hence 
orm v^2/(k\,s^2)\sim F(k,n-r) (@def-qf-noncentral-f), and the event in @eq-ci-wh-band, which is 
orm v^2\le w_k^2s^2 by Step 2, has probability 1-\alpha. (At \x= zero both sides of the inequality are zero.) Part (a) is the case \mathcal L=\C(\X\T), \mathcal U=\C(\X). Part (b). Here r=k=2 and \mathcal L=\Real^2, but the band uses only the vectors \x=(1,x)\T. The ratio in Step 2 is unchanged when \x is multiplied by a nonzero scalar, so its supremum over \{(1,x)\T:x\in\Real\} equals its supremum over all \x=(a,b)\T with a
e0. By Step 2 the supremum over all of \Real^2 is attained at \x^*=\X\T v, whose first coordinate is  one\T v. The random variable  one\T v is normal with variance \sigma^2
orm{ P_{\mathcal U} one}^2=\sigma^2n>0, because  one\in\C(\X)=\mathcal U. So with probability one \x^* has a nonzero first coordinate, the two suprema are equal, and the band event has the probability computed in Step 3. The formula for \x\T\G\x is @eq-lm-var-mean-response divided by \sigma^2. The proof has one idea: every linear function of the fitted mean is an inner product with  v, and the worst case over all directions is 
orm v. With \mathcal L=\C(\X\T) the band holds exactly when the confidence ball of @prp-ci-mean-ball contains \X beta: the band is that ball, viewed one linear functional at a time. Applied to general families of estimable functions, the argument gives Scheffé’s intervals, which Chapter 13 develops (@thm-mc-scheffe) and compares with Bonferroni and Tukey. The straight-line band is hyperbolic, narrowest at  ar{x}. Although x varies along a line, the multiplier uses k=2, because the band must hold for intercept and slope together. How much wider? The band is wider than the pointwise intervals by the factor w_k/t_{n-r,\alpha/2}, the same at every \x. The multipliers w_k=\sqrt{kF_{0.05}(k,
u)} for 95\% coverage are: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ k 
u=5 
u=10 
u=20 
u=60 
u=\infty ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ------------ 1 2.571 2.228 2.086 2.000 1.960 2 3.402 2.865 2.643 2.510 2.448 3 4.028 3.335 3.049 2.876 2.795 5 5.025 4.078 3.682 3.441 3.327 10 6.881 5.457 4.845 4.464 4.279 ------------------------------------------------------------------------ The row k=1 is the t multiplier; the column 
u=\infty is \sqrt{\chi^2_{0.05}(k)}, for known \sigma. For a straight line the band is about a quarter wider than the pointwise intervals, for ten coefficients more than twice as wide: for large k simultaneity costs roughly a factor \sqrt k. [A band for the stack loss line] Regress stack loss on air flow for the 21 days of Brownlee’s plant data (@exm-opt-stackloss-mle), ignoring the other two regressors. The fitted line is -44.132+1.0203\,x with s=4.098,  ar{x}=60.43 and S_{xx}=1681.1. The pointwise multiplier is t_{19,0.025}=2.093, and the Working–Hotelling multiplier is \sqrt{2F_{0.05}(2,19)}=2.654, larger by the factor 1.268. Figure 12.4.1 shows the data, the band, the pointwise intervals, and the 95\% prediction intervals of Section 12.3. Near the centre, at x=60, the fitted mean is 17.09, and the half-widths are 1.87 (pointwise), 2.38 (band) and 8.78 (prediction). At x=80, the edge of the data, the fitted mean is 37.49 and the half-widths are 4.50, 5.71 and 9.69. In 40000 data sets simulated from the fitted line, the band contained the true line over the whole real line in a proportion 0.9500 of the samples and over the observed range 50\le x\le80 in 0.9537. The pointwise intervals covered at x=60 in 0.9517 of the samples, but covered the line over the whole observed range in only 0.8705. [Figure 12.4.1. Stack loss against air flow: least squares line, 95\% Working–Hotelling band (solid), pointwise 95\% intervals for the mean (dashed) and pointwise 95\% prediction intervals (shaded).] Figure 12.4.1. Stack loss against air flow: least squares line, 95\% Working–Hotelling band (solid), pointwise 95\% intervals for the mean (dashed) and pointwise 95\% prediction intervals (shaded). [Stack loss against air flow: least squares line, 95\% Working–Hotelling band (solid), pointwise 95\% intervals for the mean (dashed) and pointwise 95\% prediction intervals (shaded).] Stack loss against air flow: least squares line, 95\% Working–Hotelling band (solid), pointwise 95\% intervals for the mean (dashed) and pointwise 95\% prediction intervals (shaded). import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import stats data = sm.datasets.stackloss.load_pandas().data x = data["AIRFLOW"].to_numpy() y = data["STACKLOSS"].to_numpy() n = len(y) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x]) C = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) beta_hat = C @ X.T @ y s = np.sqrt(np.sum((y - X @ beta_hat) ** 2) / (n - 2)) grid = np.linspace(45, 85, 401) Z = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(grid), grid]) fit = Z @ beta_hat se_mean = s * np.sqrt(np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Z, C, Z)) # s * sqrt(1/n + (x - xbar)^2 / Sxx) t_pt = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 2) # pointwise multiplier w_wh = np.sqrt(2 * stats.f.ppf(0.95, 2, n - 2)) # Working-Hotelling multiplier pointwise = (fit - t_pt * se_mean, fit + t_pt * se_mean) band = (fit - w_wh * se_mean, fit + w_wh * se_mean) se_new = np.sqrt(s**2 + se_mean**2) prediction = (fit - t_pt * se_new, fit + t_pt * se_new) print(f"slope {beta_hat[1]:.4f}, s = {s:.3f}; multipliers: t {t_pt:.3f}, Working-Hotelling {w_wh:.3f}") Bands over part of the space, and other shapes The band holds over the whole line. If only x\in[a,b] matters it is conservative (the simulated 0.9537), and an exact band over [a,b] uses a smaller multiplier (Wynn and Bloomfield 1971). The hyperbolic shape is also a choice: bands of constant width, or with straight edges, come from replacing the Euclidean norm in Step 2 by another norm (Gafarian 1964; Liu 2010). And if only some regressors vary, \mathcal L is smaller, and so is k. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For a straight line with many residual degrees of freedom, compute the ratio of the Working–Hotelling multiplier to the pointwise one at \alpha=0.05. How does the ratio change at \alpha=0.01? As 
u	o\infty, 2F_\alpha(2,
u)	o\chi^2_\alpha(2)=-2\log\alpha, since \chi^2(2) is exponential with mean 2. At \alpha=0.05 the ratio is \sqrt{2\log20}/z_{0.025}=2.448/1.960=1.249. At \alpha=0.01 it is \sqrt{2\log100}/z_{0.005}=3.035/2.576=1.178. The relative cost of simultaneity falls as the level becomes more demanding. As \alpha	o0, both squared multipliers, z_{\alpha/2}^2 and \chi^2_\alpha(2)=2\log(1/\alpha), grow like 2\log(1/\alpha)+O igl(\log\log(1/\alpha) igr), so the ratio of the multipliers tends to 1. [A2] For the line through the origin \E Y_i= eta x_i, show that a simultaneous band for  eta x over all real x is \hat{ eta} x\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\,s\lvert xvert/\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}, with no widening at all. Explain this with the dimension k of @thm-ci-working-hotelling. Here \C(\X\T)=\Real, so k=1 and w_1=t_{n-1,\alpha/2}. Directly: the band holds at every x iff it holds at x=1, since both sides scale with \lvert xvert. B. Practice [B1] For the straight line, show that the Working–Hotelling band contains the line b_0+b_1x for every x iff (b_0,b_1) lies in the 1-\alpha confidence ellipse for ( eta_0, eta_1) of @thm-ci-ellipsoid. Deduce that the band is the envelope of all lines whose coefficients lie in the ellipse. Put  u=(\hat{ eta}_0-b_0,\hat{ eta}_1-b_1)\T and \W=(\X\T\X)^{-1}. The line b_0+b_1x is inside the band at x iff \lvert(1,x) uvert\le w_2\,s\sqrt{(1,x)\W(1,x)\T}. By scale invariance this holds for all x iff it holds for all \mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2)\T with a_1
e0, and by continuity iff it holds for all \mathbf{a}. By @lem-ci-cauchy-schwarz that is  u\T\W^{-1} u\le w_2^2s^2, which is the ellipse. At each x, the upper edge of the band is the maximum of b_0+b_1x over the ellipse (@cor-ci-shadows), so the band is the envelope. [B2] For quadratic regression \E Y_i= eta_0+ eta_1x_i+ eta_2x_i^2, the natural band over all x uses \x=(1,x,x^2)\T, a curve in \Real^3 whose directions do not fill \Real^3. Show that the band with multiplier w_3 has coverage at least 1-\alpha over all x, and argue that its coverage is strictly larger than 1-\alpha. (Hint: when is the maximizing direction \X\T v of Step 2 a multiple of some (1,x,x^2)\T?) The band event over all \x\in\Real^3 has probability 1-\alpha and is contained in the event over the curve, so the coverage is at least 1-\alpha. Write S=
orm v^2 and S_c for the supremum of the ratio of Step 2 over the curve. The ratio depends on  v only through S and the direction  v/
orm v, so S_c=ho S, where ho\le1 is a continuous function of the direction alone. Equality ho=1 requires either that \X\T v be a multiple of some (1,x,x^2)\T, that is, its coordinates (c_0,c_1,c_2) satisfy c_0c_2=c_1^2, or that \X\T v be a multiple of (0,0,1)\T, the limit of (1,x,x^2)\T/x^2 as x	o\infty, where the supremum is approached but not attained. Both are events of probability zero. For a spherical normal vector in \mathcal U, the length and the direction are independent, and both are independent of s^2. So the coverage over the curve exceeds 1-\alpha by \Pr\{w_3^2s^2<S\le w_3^2s^2/ho\}, which is positive because S/\sigma^2 has a positive density on (0,\infty) and ho<1 almost surely. C. Going deeper [C1] A single new observation Y_0=\x_0\T beta+\varepsilon_0 will be taken at a regressor vector \x_0\in\C(\X\T) that is not known in advance. Show that the band \x\T\hbeta\pm\sqrt{(r+1)F_\alpha(r+1,n-r)}\,s\sqrt{1+\x\T\G\x}, \x\in\C(\X\T), contains Y_0 with probability at least 1-\alpha, whatever \x_0 turns out to be. (Hint: apply Step 2 of the proof to the (r+1)-dimensional vector ( v,\varepsilon_0).) For \x=\X\T u with  u\in\C(\X), Y_0-\x\T\hbeta=\varepsilon_0- u\T v, with  v=\M(\Y-\X beta), and 1+\x\T\G\x=1+
orm u^2. By Cauchy–Schwarz in \C(\X)	imes\Real, (\varepsilon_0- u\T v)^2\le(1+
orm u^2)(\varepsilon_0^2+
orm v^2). The variable (\varepsilon_0^2+
orm v^2)/\sigma^2 is \chi^2(r+1), independent of SSE, so (\varepsilon_0^2+
orm v^2)/((r+1)s^2)\sim F(r+1,n-r), and on the event that it is at most F_\alpha(r+1,n-r), which has probability 1-\alpha, the band contains Y_0 at every \x, in particular at \x_0. [C2] Two straight lines are fitted in one model, with separate intercepts and slopes and a common \sigma^2. Construct simultaneous bands for both lines with joint coverage at least 1-\alpha in two ways: (i) @thm-ci-working-hotelling with \mathcal L=\Real^4, (ii) a band for each line with \mathcal L=\Real^2 at level \alpha/2, combined by the Bonferroni inequality. Compare the multipliers for n-r=20 and explain which is better and why.

title: 12.5 Inverse prediction and calibration
content:
Inverse prediction and calibration Prediction runs from x to y. Calibration runs the other way: an instrument is calibrated on specimens of known value, a new specimen is measured, and its value is wanted. The estimate reads the fitted line backwards; the interval reads the prediction band backwards, and it is not always an interval. Ratios of estimable functions Inverse prediction belongs to a wider problem: a confidence set for a ratio of linear functions of the coefficients, such as the zero crossing - eta_0/ eta_1 of a line or the turning point - eta_1/(2 eta_2) of a quadratic. A delta-method interval ignores that the denominator is uncertain and may be near zero. Fieller’s approach tests, for each candidate value, a hypothesis that is linear in the coefficients. [Fieller’s confidence set for a ratio] Let  lambda_1, lambda_2\in\C(\X\T) be linearly independent, put a= lambda_1\T beta, b= lambda_2\T beta, their estimates \hat{a}= lambda_1\T\hbeta, \hat{b}= lambda_2\T\hbeta, and v_{ij}= lambda_i\T\G lambda_j, so that \mathbf{V}=(v_{ij}) is positive definite. Suppose b
e0 and let 	heta=a/b. With t=t_{n-r,\alpha/2}, let  egin{aligned} \mathcal F(\Y)= igl\{	heta_0\in\Real:\ &(\hat{a}-	heta_0\hat{b})^2\ &\le t^2s^2\,(v_{11}-2	heta_0v_{12}+	heta_0^2v_{22}) igr\}. \end{aligned} {#eq-ci-fieller} 1. \mathcal F(\Y) is an exact 1-\alpha confidence set for 	heta, at every parameter value with b
e0. 2. Let Q=(\hat{a},\hat{b})\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\hat{a},\hat{b})\T. Outside an event of probability zero, \mathcal F(\Y) is - a bounded closed interval containing \hat{	heta}=\hat{a}/\hat{b}, if \hat{b}^2>t^2s^2v_{22}; - the union of two disjoint closed rays, if \hat{b}^2<t^2s^2v_{22} and Q>t^2s^2; - the whole real line, if \hat{b}^2<t^2s^2v_{22} and Q<t^2s^2. (a) Fix 	heta_0. The vector  lambda_1-	heta_0 lambda_2 lies in \C(\X\T) and is not zero, so ( lambda_1-	heta_0 lambda_2)\T beta=a-	heta_0b is estimable, with estimate \hat{a}-	heta_0\hat{b} and ( lambda_1-	heta_0 lambda_2)\T\G( lambda_1-	heta_0 lambda_2)=v_{11}-2	heta_0v_{12}+	heta_0^2v_{22}. The inequality in @eq-ci-fieller says that the t interval of @thm-ci-estimable-interval for a-	heta_0b contains 0. At 	heta_0=	heta, a-	heta b=0, so the probability of this event is exactly 1-\alpha. (b) The defining inequality is q(	heta_0)=A	heta_0^2-2B	heta_0+K\le0, with A=\hat{b}^2-t^2s^2v_{22},\qquad B=\hat{a}\hat{b}-t^2s^2v_{12},\qquad K=\hat{a}^2-t^2s^2v_{11}. Expanding and using (\hat{a},\hat{b})\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\hat{a},\hat{b})\T=(v_{22}\hat{a}^2-2v_{12}\hat{a}\hat{b}+v_{11}\hat{b}^2)/\det\mathbf{V},  egin{aligned} B^2-AK&=t^2s^2 igl(v_{22}\hat{a}^2-2v_{12}\hat{a}\hat{b}+v_{11}\hat{b}^2-t^2s^2\det\mathbf{V} igr)\ &=t^2s^2\det(\mathbf{V})\,(Q-t^2s^2). \end{aligned} If A>0, then q(\hat{	heta})=-t^2s^2(v_{11}-2\hat{	heta} v_{12}+\hat{	heta}^2v_{22})<0, so the upward parabola q has two real roots, and \{q\le0\} is the closed interval between them, which contains \hat{	heta}. If A<0, the parabola opens downward. When B^2-AK<0 it is negative everywhere and \mathcal F(\Y)=\Real. When B^2-AK>0 it is nonpositive exactly outside the open interval between its roots. The events A=0 and Q=t^2s^2 have probability zero, because \hat{b} and Q/s^2 have continuous distributions. The first case says that the t test rejects b=0: the denominator is away from zero and the ratio is confined. Otherwise very large \lvert	hetavert cannot be excluded, and Q/(2s^2), the F statistic for a=b=0, decides between two rays and the whole line. @exr-ci-fieller-geometry gives a picture: \mathcal F(\Y) is the set of slopes of lines through the origin that meet a certain confidence ellipse for (a,b). The calibration problem A calibration experiment measures n standards with known values x_1,\dots,x_n, not all equal, and records readings Y_i= eta_0+ eta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,n . A new specimen with unknown value x_0 is then measured m\ge1 times, Y_{0j}= eta_0+ eta_1x_0+\varepsilon_{0j}, and all n+m errors are independent \Normal(0,\sigma^2). Let  ar{Y}_0 be the mean of the new readings, and let \hat{ eta}_0, \hat{ eta}_1 and s^2 (with n-2 degrees of freedom) come from the standards alone. The classical estimator reads the fitted line backwards: \hat{x}_0= rac{ ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0}{\hat{ eta}_1}= ar{x}+ rac{ ar{Y}_0- ar{Y}}{\hat{ eta}_1}. It is the maximum likelihood estimator (@exr-ci-calibration-mle) and, being a ratio, inherits a pathology of ratios. [The classical estimator has no mean] If \Pr( ar{Y}_0
e ar{Y})>0, which always holds here, then \E\lvert\hat{x}_0vert=\infty.  ar{Y} and \hat{ eta}_1 are jointly normal and uncorrelated (@cor-lm-simple-moments), hence independent (@thm-mvn-independence), and  ar{Y}_0 is independent of both. So g= ar{Y}_0- ar{Y} is independent of \hat{ eta}_1 and \E\lvert\hat{x}_0- ar{x}vert=\E\lvert gvert\,\E\lvert1/\hat{ eta}_1vert, with \E\lvert gvert>0. The density f of \hat{ eta}_1 is continuous and positive at 0, so f\ge c>0 on some [-\epsilon,\epsilon] and \E\lvert1/\hat{ eta}_1vert\ge c\int_{-\epsilon}^{\epsilon}\lvert uvert^{-1}\,du=\infty. Finally \lvert\hat{x}_0vert\ge\lvert\hat{x}_0- ar{x}vert-\lvert ar{x}vert. So a delta-method “standard error” of \hat{x}_0 approximates a quantity that does not exist. That is harmless when \hat{ eta}_1 is many standard errors from zero, and harmful exactly when the slope is poorly determined. [Calibration set] In the calibration model, let t=t_{n-2,\alpha/2} and  egin{aligned} \mathcal C=\Bigl\{x\in\Real:\ & igl( ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0-\hat{ eta}_1x igr)^2\ &\le t^2s^2\Bigl( rac1m+ rac1n+ rac{(x- ar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Bigr)\Bigr\}. \end{aligned} {#eq-ci-calibration} 1. \mathcal C is an exact 1-\alpha confidence set for x_0, at every ( eta_0, eta_1,\sigma^2,x_0), including  eta_1=0. 2. \mathcal C is the set of x at which  ar{Y}_0 lies inside the 1-\alpha prediction interval of @thm-ci-prediction-interval(c) for the mean of m new readings at x. 3. Let T_1=\hat{ eta}_1\sqrt{S_{xx}}/s be the t statistic for the slope and g= ar{Y}_0- ar{Y}. Outside an event of probability zero, \mathcal C is - a bounded interval containing \hat{x}_0, if T_1^2>t^2; - the union of two disjoint closed rays, if T_1^2<t^2 and T_1^2+g^2/\{s^2(1/m+1/n)\}>t^2; - the whole real line, if T_1^2+g^2/\{s^2(1/m+1/n)\}<t^2. (a) and (b). For fixed x,  ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0-\hat{ eta}_1x is the difference between the mean of the new readings and the estimated mean response at x. At x=x_0, @thm-ci-prediction-interval(c), with \x_0=(1,x_0)\T and h_0=1/n+(x_0- ar{x})^2/S_{xx} (@eq-lm-var-mean-response), shows that  rac{ ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0-\hat{ eta}_1x_0}{s\sqrt{1/m+1/n+(x_0- ar{x})^2/S_{xx}}}\sim t(n-2), whatever the parameters are. This is a pivot, and x_0\in\mathcal C is the event that its absolute value is at most t. Nothing in the argument requires  eta_1
e0. Part (b) restates the definition. (b) Put d=x- ar{x} and c=1/m+1/n. Since  ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0-\hat{ eta}_1x=g-\hat{ eta}_1d, the defining inequality is Ad^2-2\hat{ eta}_1g\,d+(g^2-t^2s^2c)\le0 with A=\hat{ eta}_1^2-t^2s^2/S_{xx}. Its discriminant is  egin{aligned} \hat{ eta}_1^2g^2-A(g^2-t^2s^2c)&=t^2s^2\Bigl( rac{g^2}{S_{xx}}+cA\Bigr)\ &= rac{t^2s^4c}{S_{xx}}\Bigl(T_1^2+ rac{g^2}{s^2c}-t^2\Bigr). \end{aligned} The sign of A is that of T_1^2-t^2. If A>0, the quadratic is negative at d=g/\hat{ eta}_1, that is at x=\hat{x}_0, where it equals -t^2s^2(c+d^2/S_{xx}); so it has two real roots and \mathcal C is the interval between them. If A<0, the argument of @prp-ci-fieller(b) applies: two rays if the discriminant is positive and the whole line if it is negative. Equalities have probability zero. Part (b) is the practical recipe (Figure 12.5.1): draw the prediction band for the mean of m readings and the horizontal line at  ar{Y}_0, and read off where the line is inside the band. A steep calibration line crosses the band in a short interval. A flat one lets both hyperbolic edges pass the horizontal line, giving two rays or everything. The set is bounded iff the slope test rejects, as it does for any useful instrument. [Unbounded calibration sets cannot be avoided] Let \mathcal D be any confidence set for x_0 with coverage at least 1-\alpha>0 at every parameter value, including those with  eta_1=0. Then at every parameter value with  eta_1=0, \Pr\{v\in\mathcal D\}\ge1-\alpha for every real v, and if \mathcal D is measurable in the sense of @prp-ci-nonestimable, its expected length is infinite. When  eta_1=0, the joint distribution of the standards and the new readings does not involve x_0. So for every v, the probability that v\in\mathcal D is the same as it would be if x_0 were v, and that probability is at least 1-\alpha. The rest is the Fubini argument in the proof of @prp-ci-nonestimable. By continuity the same happens approximately for small  eta_1. A procedure that always reports a bounded interval, like the delta method, pays with coverage below 1-\alpha somewhere. The Fieller set’s unbounded answers are the honest answer to a question the data cannot settle. [Calibrating an assay] In a simulated assay, nine standards of concentration 0,1,\dots,8 are each measured three times (n=27). The fitted line is 0.0338+0.1161\,x, with s=0.0131 and slope t statistic 118.7. A new specimen is read m=3 times, with mean reading 0.6521. The classical estimate is \hat{x}_0=5.327, and the 95\% calibration interval is (5.184,\ 5.471) (t_{25,0.025}=2.060). For an assay this precise the delta-method interval, \hat{x}_0\pm t\,(s/\lvert\hat{ eta}_1vert)\sqrt{1/m+1/n+(\hat{x}_0- ar{x})^2/S_{xx}}, agrees to three decimals: (5.184,\ 5.471). Now consider a weak assay with the same design, in which the fitted slope is 0.0021 and its t statistic is only 1.67. The mean reading of the standards is 0.0475. A specimen with mean reading 0.0525, close to that mean, gives the whole real line: nothing about its concentration can be concluded. A specimen with mean reading 0.0775 gives two rays, (-\infty,\ -55.3]\cup[7.6,\ \infty): the middle of the scale is excluded, but not extreme concentrations of either sign. Figure 12.5.1 shows both assays. In 20000 simulated experiments at x_0=5.3, both intervals cover in 0.9517 for the precise assay. With the slope three standard errors from zero ( eta_1=0.00335) the Fieller set again covers in 0.9517, since its event involves only the errors, and is bounded in 0.817 of the experiments, close to the power 0.822 of the slope t test; the delta-method interval covers in 0.9827, wastefully. With the slope two standard errors from zero and x_0=12, beyond the standards, the Fieller set covers in 0.9528 and the delta-method interval in only 0.9337. [Figure 12.5.1. Calibration inverts the 95\% prediction band for the mean of m=3 readings (shaded); bars mark the calibration sets for the observed readings (horizontal lines). (a) A precise assay, magnified in the inset. (b) A weak assay: whole line (lower bar) and two rays (upper bar).] Figure 12.5.1. Calibration inverts the 95\% prediction band for the mean of m=3 readings (shaded); bars mark the calibration sets for the observed readings (horizontal lines). (a) A precise assay, magnified in the inset. (b) A weak assay: whole line (lower bar) and two rays (upper bar). [Calibration inverts the 95\% prediction band for the mean of m=3 readings (shaded); bars mark the calibration sets for the observed readings (horizontal lines). (a) A precise assay, magnified in the inset. (b) A weak assay: whole line (lower bar) and two rays (upper bar).] Calibration inverts the 95\% prediction band for the mean of m=3 readings (shaded); bars mark the calibration sets for the observed readings (horizontal lines). (a) A precise assay, magnified in the inset. (b) A weak assay: whole line (lower bar) and two rays (upper bar). import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(1206) x = np.repeat(np.arange(9.0), 3) # standards, in triplicate n = len(x) y = 0.04 + 0.115 * x + 0.015 * rng.normal(size=n) # absorbance readings m = 3 y0 = 0.04 + 0.115 * 5.3 + 0.015 * rng.normal(size=m) # the unknown sample, true x0 = 5.3 def calibrate(x, y, y0bar, m, level=0.95): """Fieller set {x0 : |y0bar - b0 - b1 x0| <= t s sqrt(1/m + 1/n + (x0 - xbar)^2 / Sxx)}.""" n = len(x) xbar, Sxx = x.mean(), np.sum((x - x.mean()) ** 2) b1 = np.sum((x - xbar) * (y - y.mean())) / Sxx s2 = np.sum((y - y.mean() - b1 * (x - xbar)) ** 2) / (n - 2) t2 = stats.t.ppf(0.5 + level / 2, n - 2) ** 2 g = y0bar - y.mean() # quadratic in d = x0 - xbar: A d^2 - 2 B d + K <= 0 A = b1**2 - t2 * s2 / Sxx B = b1 * g K = g**2 - t2 * s2 * (1 / m + 1 / n) disc = B**2 - A * K if disc < 0: return "whole line", (-np.inf, np.inf), xbar + g / b1 r1, r2 = sorted([(B - np.sqrt(disc)) / A, (B + np.sqrt(disc)) / A]) if A > 0: return "interval", (xbar + r1, xbar + r2), xbar + g / b1 return "two rays", (xbar + r1, xbar + r2), xbar + g / b1 # (-inf, first] and [second, inf) shape, (lo, hi), x0_hat = calibrate(x, y, y0.mean(), m) print(f"estimate {x0_hat:.3f}; 95% calibration set: {shape} ({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})") [Classical or inverse estimation?] The inverse estimator regresses the x_i on the readings and predicts from  ar{Y}_0: 	ilde{x}_0= ar{x}+(S_{xy}/S_{yy})( ar{Y}_0- ar{Y}), with S_{xy}=\sum(x_i- ar{x})(Y_i- ar{Y}) and S_{yy}=\sum(Y_i- ar{Y})^2. Since  ar{Y}_0- ar{Y}=\hat{ eta}_1(\hat{x}_0- ar{x}) and \hat{ eta}_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}, 	ilde{x}_0- ar{x}= rac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}(\hat{x}_0- ar{x})=R^2(\hat{x}_0- ar{x}), where R is the sample correlation of the calibration pairs. So 	ilde{x}_0 shrinks \hat{x}_0 toward  ar{x} by the factor R^2\in[0,1]. It has finite moments and can beat \hat{x}_0 in mean squared error near the centre of the standards (Krutchkoff 1967); away from the centre it does worse (@exr-ci-inverse-estimator). Hoadley (1970) showed that it is a Bayes estimator under a particular prior for x_0. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] For a straight line, write down Fieller’s 1-\alpha confidence set for the point \xi=- eta_0/ eta_1 where the line crosses zero, and state the condition under which it is a bounded interval. Show that it is the calibration set of @thm-ci-calibration with  ar{Y}_0 replaced by 0 and 1/m replaced by 0. With  lambda_1=(1,0)\T and  lambda_2=(0,1)\T, \xi=-a/b. Apply @prp-ci-fieller to 	heta=a/b and change sign, or directly: \xi_0 is in the set iff the t interval for  eta_0+ eta_1\xi_0 contains 0, that is iff (\hat{ eta}_0+\hat{ eta}_1\xi_0)^2\le t^2s^2\{1/n+(\xi_0- ar{x})^2/S_{xx}\}. This is @eq-ci-calibration with  ar{Y}_0=0 and the 1/m term absent, because 0 is a known number rather than an average of new readings. It is bounded iff T_1^2>t^2. [A2] Show that \hat{x}_0, together with the least squares estimates from the standards, maximizes the joint likelihood of the n+m readings over ( eta_0, eta_1,\sigma^2,x_0) when \hat{ eta}_1
e0. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of \sigma^2? For fixed \sigma^2 the likelihood is maximized by minimizing \sum_i(Y_i- eta_0- eta_1x_i)^2+\sum_j(Y_{0j}- eta_0- eta_1x_0)^2. For any  eta_1
e0 the second sum is minimized over x_0 by choosing  eta_0+ eta_1x_0= ar{Y}_0, leaving \sum_j(Y_{0j}- ar{Y}_0)^2, which is free of the parameters. The first sum is then minimized by least squares on the standards, and x_0=( ar{Y}_0-\hat{ eta}_0)/\hat{ eta}_1=\hat{x}_0. The maximum likelihood estimate of \sigma^2 is \{	ext{SSE}+\sum_j(Y_{0j}- ar{Y}_0)^2\}/(n+m). B. Practice [B1] When m\ge2, the new readings carry their own information about \sigma^2. Let s_p^2=\{	ext{SSE}+\sum_j(Y_{0j}- ar{Y}_0)^2\}/(n+m-3). Show that replacing s by s_p and t_{n-2,\alpha/2} by t_{n+m-3,\alpha/2} in @eq-ci-calibration gives another exact 1-\alpha set. Why is it shorter on average, and why is it more often bounded? The within-specimen sum of squares is \sigma^2\chi^2(m-1), independent of  ar{Y}_0 (the sample mean and sample variance of a normal sample are independent) and of the standards. So \{	ext{SSE}+\sum_j(Y_{0j}- ar{Y}_0)^2\}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n+m-3), independent of the numerator of the pivot, and the pivot with s_p is t(n+m-3). More degrees of freedom give a smaller multiplier and a less variable estimate of \sigma, so the set is shorter on average. The bounded case requires \hat{ eta}_1^2S_{xx}>t^2s_p^2, and a smaller t makes this easier. [B2] In the quadratic regression \E Y_i= eta_0+ eta_1x_i+ eta_2x_i^2, use @prp-ci-fieller to give a confidence set for the location x^*=- eta_1/(2 eta_2) of the turning point. When is it a bounded interval, and what does that condition mean for the curvature? Take  lambda_1=(0,1,0)\T,  lambda_2=(0,0,2)\T and 	heta= eta_1/(2 eta_2), so x^*=-	heta. The set is \{x_0:(\hat{ eta}_1+2\hat{ eta}_2x_0)^2\le t^2s^2(c_{11}+4c_{12}x_0+4c_{22}x_0^2)\}, where c_{ij} are the entries of (\X\T\X)^{-1} belonging to  eta_1, eta_2. It is the set of x_0 at which the estimated derivative  eta_1+2 eta_2x_0 is not significantly different from zero. It is bounded iff \hat{ eta}_2^2>t^2s^2c_{22}, that is iff the curvature is significant: without significant curvature, the fitted curve may be nearly straight and its turning point anywhere. [B3] Study the two estimators of the Remark “Classical or inverse estimation?” in an idealized large calibration experiment: the standards are so numerous that \hat{ eta}_0, \hat{ eta}_1 and R^2 may be replaced by constants  eta_0,  eta_1
e0 and ho^2\in(0,1), while  ar{Y}_0 is still the mean of m new readings. Let v=\sigma^2/(m eta_1^2). 1. Show that \hat{x}_0 is unbiased with mean squared error v, and that 	ilde{x}_0= ar{x}+ho^2(\hat{x}_0- ar{x}) has mean squared error ho^4v+(1-ho^2)^2(x_0- ar{x})^2. 2. Show that 	ilde{x}_0 has the smaller mean squared error iff (x_0- ar{x})^2<v(1+ho^2)/(1-ho^2). 3. Let 	au^2=S_{xx}/n, so that in this limit ho^2= eta_1^2	au^2/( eta_1^2	au^2+\sigma^2). Show that the condition of part 2 reads (x_0- ar{x})^2<v+2	au^2/m. With m=1 and a precise instrument, roughly how far from  ar{x}, in units of the spread 	au of the standards, does the inverse estimator stay ahead? 1. Here \hat{x}_0=x_0+ ar{\varepsilon}_0/ eta_1 with  ar{\varepsilon}_0\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2/m), so it is unbiased with variance v. Then 	ilde{x}_0-x_0=ho^2(\hat{x}_0-x_0)-(1-ho^2)(x_0- ar{x}): variance ho^4v plus squared bias (1-ho^2)^2(x_0- ar{x})^2. 2. The inequality ho^4v+(1-ho^2)^2(x_0- ar{x})^2<v is (1-ho^2)^2(x_0- ar{x})^2<(1-ho^2)(1+ho^2)v; divide by (1-ho^2)^2>0. 3. (1+ho^2)/(1-ho^2)=(2 eta_1^2	au^2+\sigma^2)/\sigma^2, so v(1+ho^2)/(1-ho^2)=v+2	au^2/m. When \sigma is small, v\approx0 and the inverse estimator wins only for \lvert x_0- ar{x}vert<\sqrt2\,	au, a little more than one spread from the centre; beyond that its bias dominates. C. Going deeper [C1] In the setting of @prp-ci-fieller, let E_t=\{ oldsymbol{\phi}\in\Real^2:((\hat{a},\hat{b})\T- oldsymbol{\phi})\T\mathbf{V}^{-1}((\hat{a},\hat{b})\T- oldsymbol{\phi})\le t^2s^2\}, an ellipse with the t constant in place of 2F_\alpha(2,n-r). Show that 	heta_0\in\mathcal F(\Y) iff the line \{(\phi_1,\phi_2):\phi_1=	heta_0\phi_2\} meets E_t. Use the picture to explain the three cases: the set is the whole line iff E_t contains the origin, and it is bounded iff E_t does not meet the axis \phi_2=0. The line is \{ oldsymbol{\phi}:\mathbf{c}\T oldsymbol{\phi}=0\} with \mathbf{c}=(1,-	heta_0)\T. By @cor-ci-shadows (with the constant t^2s^2), the values of \mathbf{c}\T oldsymbol{\phi} over E_t form the interval \hat{a}-	heta_0\hat{b}\pm ts\sqrt{\mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{c}}, and \mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{c}=v_{11}-2	heta_0v_{12}+	heta_0^2v_{22}. So the line meets E_t iff this interval contains 0, which is @eq-ci-fieller. Every line through the origin meets E_t iff the origin is in E_t, which is Q\le t^2s^2. Lines of large slope approach the axis \phi_2=0 (the \phi_1-axis in these coordinates); the set is unbounded iff lines of arbitrarily large slope meet E_t, iff E_t meets that axis, which by @cor-ci-shadows with \mathbf{c}=(0,1)\T is \hat{b}^2\le t^2s^2v_{22}. [C2] Two straight lines \E Y=\alpha_k+ eta_kx, k=1,2, are fitted to two independent samples in one model with a common \sigma^2, as in a two-phase regression. Use @prp-ci-fieller to construct a confidence set for the x-coordinate (\alpha_1-\alpha_2)/( eta_2- eta_1) of their intersection. When is it bounded? Interpret the unbounded cases in terms of parallel lines.

title: 12.6 Bayesian thread II: credible intervals and predictive distributions
content: Bayesian thread II: credible intervals and predictive distributions Section 7.6 derived the posterior distribution of ( beta,\sigma^2) under the conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior, and showed that the flat prior \pi( beta,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2 reproduces least squares. Here the posterior is summarized by credible regions and used to predict. In the conjugate model these have the shapes of the frequentist sets, and under the flat prior they coincide with them. We end by asking how often a credible interval covers in repeated sampling. Credible sets [Credible set] Let heta be a function of the parameters and let \pi(\cdot\mid\y) be its posterior distribution. A set C(\y) with \Pr\{ heta\in C(\y)\mid\y\}\ge1-\alpha is a 1-\alpha credible set for heta. If the posterior has a density \pi( heta\mid\y), a set of the form \{ heta:\pi( heta\mid\y)\ge k\} with posterior probability 1-\alpha is a highest posterior density (HPD) set. Here the statement concerns the realized set. An HPD set has the smallest volume among sets with its posterior probability. We need three facts about the multivariate t distribution of @def-opt-mvt. [Multivariate t] Let u\sim t_ u(\mathbf{m}, S) in \Real^p, with S positive definite. 1. If \A is q imes p of rank q, then \A u\sim t_ u(\A\mathbf{m},\A S\A\T). 2. ( u-\mathbf{m})\T S^{-1}( u-\mathbf{m})/p\sim F(p, u). 3. u has density proportional to igl\{1+( u-\mathbf{m})\T S^{-1}( u-\mathbf{m})/ u igr\}^{-( u+p)/2}. By @def-opt-mvt, u=\mathbf{m}+\Z/\sqrt{W/ u} with \Z\sim\Normal_p( zero, S) and W\sim\chi^2( u) independent. (a) \A u=\A\mathbf{m}+\A\Z/\sqrt{W/ u}, and \A\Z\sim\Normal_q( zero,\A S\A\T) (@thm-mvn-linear) is independent of W, with \A S\A\T positive definite. (b) ( u-\mathbf{m})\T S^{-1}( u-\mathbf{m})=\Z\T S^{-1}\Z/(W/ u), and \Z\T S^{-1}\Z\sim\chi^2(p) independently of W (@cor-qf-mahalanobis(a)). Divide by p and use @def-qf-noncentral-f. (c) Given W=w, u\sim\Normal_p(\mathbf{m},( u/w) S). Write D=( u-\mathbf{m})\T S^{-1}( u-\mathbf{m}). Integrating the normal density (@thm-mvn-density) against the \chi^2( u) density of W, and dropping factors free of u, egin{aligned} \int_0^\infty w^{p/2}e^{-wD/(2 u)}\,w^{ u/2-1}e^{-w/2}\,dw &=\int_0^\infty w^{( u+p)/2-1}e^{-w(1+D/ u)/2}\,dw\ &\propto(1+D/ u)^{-( u+p)/2}, \end{aligned} by the substitution w'=w(1+D/ u). Credible sets and predictive distributions in the conjugate model [Credible sets and posterior predictive distribution] Let the prior be ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m}_0,\V_0,a_0,b_0), so that by @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate the posterior is ext{NIG}(\mathbf{m}_n,\V_n,a_n,b_n). Put u=2a_n and au^2=b_n/a_n. 1. For lambda e zero, the interval lambda\T\mathbf{m}_n\ \pm\ t_{ u,\alpha/2}\, au\sqrt{ lambda\T\V_n lambda} is the 1-\alpha HPD credible interval for lambda\T beta; it is also equal-tailed. 2. For a p imes q matrix Lambda of rank q, the set egin{aligned} igl\{ oldsymbol{\phi}_0:\ &( oldsymbol{\phi}_0- Lambda\T\mathbf{m}_n)\T( Lambda\T\V_n Lambda)^{-1}( oldsymbol{\phi}_0- Lambda\T\mathbf{m}_n)\ &\le q\, au^2F_\alpha(q, u) igr\} \end{aligned} is the 1-\alpha HPD credible region for Lambda\T beta. 3. Let \mathbf{Y}_0=\X_0 beta+ e_0 be k future observations, with e_0\sim\Normal_k( zero,\sigma^2\I_k) independent of \Y and of beta given \sigma^2. The posterior predictive distribution of \mathbf{Y}_0 is \mathbf{Y}_0\mid\y\ \sim\ t_ u igl(\X_0\mathbf{m}_n,\ au^2(\I_k+\X_0\V_n\X_0\T) igr). In particular, for one future observation at \x_0, the interval \x_0\T\mathbf{m}_n\pm t_{ u,\alpha/2}\, au\sqrt{1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0} has posterior predictive probability 1-\alpha. 4. igl[2b_n/\chi^2_{\alpha/2}( u),\ 2b_n/\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}( u) igr] is an equal-tailed 1-\alpha credible interval for \sigma^2. By @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate and @lem-opt-nig-marginal, beta\mid\y\sim t_ u(\mathbf{m}_n, au^2\V_n) and 2b_n/\sigma^2\mid\y\sim\chi^2( u). (a) By @lem-ci-mvt(a) with \A= lambda\T, lambda\T beta= lambda\T\mathbf{m}_n+ au\sqrt{ lambda\T\V_n lambda}\,T with T\sim t( u). The t( u) density is symmetric and decreasing in \lvert x vert, so the symmetric interval is both equal-tailed and HPD. (b) By @lem-ci-mvt(a), Lambda\T beta\mid\y\sim t_ u( Lambda\T\mathbf{m}_n, au^2 Lambda\T\V_n Lambda). By (b) of the lemma the quadratic form divided by q au^2 is F(q, u), so the set has posterior probability 1-\alpha. By (c) the density is a decreasing function of the quadratic form, so the set has the form \{ ext{density}\ge k\}. (c) Given \sigma^2 and \y, beta\sim\Normal_p(\mathbf{m}_n,\sigma^2\V_n) and e_0\sim\Normal_k( zero,\sigma^2\I_k) independently, so \mathbf{Y}_0\sim\Normal_k igl(\X_0\mathbf{m}_n,\sigma^2(\X_0\V_n\X_0\T+\I_k) igr) (@thm-mvn-linear). Together with \sigma^2\mid\y\sim ext{IG}(a_n,b_n), this says that (\mathbf{Y}_0,\sigma^2)\mid\y is ext{NIG} igl(\X_0\mathbf{m}_n,\I_k+\X_0\V_n\X_0\T,a_n,b_n igr) (@def-opt-nig), the matrix being positive definite. @lem-opt-nig-marginal gives the t_ u law, and (a) of the present theorem, applied to it with k=1, gives the interval. (d) \Pr\{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}( u)\le2b_n/\sigma^2\le\chi^2_{\alpha/2}( u)\mid\y\}=1-\alpha; invert the inequalities. The formulas mirror the frequentist ones: \hbeta becomes \mathbf{m}_n, \G becomes \V_n=(\V_0^{-1}+\X\T\X)^{-1}, s^2 becomes au^2, and n-r becomes u=2a_0+n, which counts every observation plus 2a_0 “prior observations” about \sigma^2. The 1 in 1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0 is again the new error. [The flat prior reproduces the frequentist sets] Let ank(\X)=p0, and let the prior be \pi( beta,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2. Then the credible interval (a), the region (b), the predictive interval (c) and the interval for \sigma^2 (d) of @thm-ci-bayes-credible are, respectively, the t interval of @thm-ci-estimable-interval, the confidence ellipsoid of @thm-ci-ellipsoid, the prediction interval of @thm-ci-prediction-interval and the interval of @prp-ci-sigma. By @cor-opt-flat-prior the posterior is ext{NIG} igl(\hbeta,(\X\T\X)^{-1},(n-p)/2, ext{SSE}/2 igr). The proof of @thm-ci-bayes-credible used only that the posterior is normal-inverse-gamma, so its conclusions hold with \mathbf{m}_n=\hbeta, \V_n=(\X\T\X)^{-1}=\G, u=n-p=n-r, au^2= ext{SSE}/(n-p)=s^2 and 2b_n= ext{SSE}. Substituting gives the four frequentist sets. The same set then carries two readings: “this procedure covers the fixed truth in 95\% of samples” and “given these data, the parameter lies here with probability 0.95”. The agreement is special; it fails for proper priors and for most other models. A worked example [Predicting a day of stack loss] Take the stack loss regression with the engineer’s prior of @exm-opt-stackloss-bayes, and consider a new day with air flow 65, water temperature 23 and acid concentration 87. The posterior has a_n=13.5, so u=27 and t_{27,0.025}=2.052. By @thm-ci-bayes-credible, the 95\% credible interval for the mean stack loss at these conditions is 23.12\pm1.51, and the 95\% posterior predictive interval for the day’s stack loss is 23.12\pm6.11. The least squares answers are 23.15\pm1.77 for the mean and 23.15\pm7.07 for the new day, with t_{17,0.025}=2.110. The Bayesian intervals are shorter because the prior informs the slopes, shrinking \x_0\T\V_n\x_0, and \sigma^2, raising the degrees of freedom from 17 to 27. The 2.5\% and 97.5\% points of 400000 posterior predictive draws are 17.00 and 29.21, matching the t interval within Monte Carlo error. The simulated posterior probability of the credible ellipse of (b) for the air-flow and water-temperature coefficients is 0.9503. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy import stats data = sm.datasets.stackloss.load_pandas().data y = data["STACKLOSS"].to_numpy() X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), data[["AIRFLOW", "WATERTEMP", "ACIDCONC"]]]) n, p = X.shape XtX, Xty = X.T @ X, X.T @ y def nig_posterior(m0, P0, a0, b0, y=y): """Conjugate update; P0 is the prior precision V0^{-1} (per unit sigma^2).""" Vn = np.linalg.inv(P0 + XtX) mn = Vn @ (P0 @ m0 + X.T @ y) an = a0 + n / 2 bn = b0 + (y @ y + m0 @ P0 @ m0 - mn @ (P0 + XtX) @ mn) / 2 return mn, Vn, an, bn m0 = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # the prior of Chapter 7 P0 = np.linalg.inv(np.diag([100.0**2, 0.1**2, 0.2**2, 0.1**2])) a0, b0 = 3.0, 18.0 mn, Vn, an, bn = nig_posterior(m0, P0, a0, b0) x0 = np.array([1.0, 65.0, 23.0, 87.0]) # a new operating condition qb = stats.t.ppf(0.975, 2 * an) centre = x0 @ mn half_mean = qb * np.sqrt(bn / an * (x0 @ Vn @ x0)) # credible interval for x0^T beta half_new = qb * np.sqrt(bn / an * (1 + x0 @ Vn @ x0)) # posterior predictive interval for Y0 beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(XtX, Xty) # frequentist intervals, for comparison s2 = np.sum((y - X @ beta_hat) ** 2) / (n - p) qf = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - p) h0 = x0 @ np.linalg.solve(XtX, x0) print(f"Bayes: mean response {centre:.2f} +- {half_mean:.2f}; new day {centre:.2f} +- {half_new:.2f}") print(f"least squares: mean response {x0 @ beta_hat:.2f} +- {qf * np.sqrt(s2 * h0):.2f}; " f"new day +- {qf * np.sqrt(s2 * (1 + h0)):.2f}") How often does a credible interval cover? One coverage statement holds for every proper prior. [Coverage averaged over the prior] Let the prior \pi be proper, and let C(\y) be a 1-\alpha credible set for heta for every \y. If ( beta,\sigma^2) is drawn from \pi and then \Y from the model, \Pr\{ heta\in C(\Y)\}\ge1-\alpha, with equality if every C(\y) has posterior probability exactly 1-\alpha. Equivalently, the frequentist coverage \Pr_{ beta,\sigma^2}\{ heta\in C(\Y)\}, averaged over \pi, is at least 1-\alpha. Under the joint distribution of parameters and data, the conditional distribution of the parameters given \Y=\y is the posterior. By the tower property, \Pr\{ heta\in C(\Y)\}=\E igl[\Pr\{ heta\in C(\Y)\mid\Y\} igr]\ge1-\alpha. Conditioning instead on the parameters gives the second form. The average hides variation: coverage is high where the prior is right and low where it is wrong. Consider the credible interval for the air-flow coefficient in @exm-ci-stackloss-predictive, and simulate its frequentist coverage when the true air-flow coefficient is varied, the other coefficients are held at their least squares values, and \sigma^2=s^2. Figure 12.6.1 shows the result. With the prior of Chapter 7, the coverage is 0.959 when the truth is the prior mean 1, and 0.936 at 0.7 and at 1.5. It ranges from 0.877 to 0.965 over the plotted range. This prior is mild, and prior–data conflict inflates b_n, which widens the interval. A prior with slope standard deviations five times smaller behaves very differently: its coverage is 1.000 at the prior mean but 0.007 at 0.7, close to the least squares estimate, and 0.000 at 1.5. Averaged over the prior of Chapter 7, the simulated coverage is 0.9512 (40000 draws), as @prp-ci-average-coverage requires. The flat-prior interval is the t interval and covers exactly 95\% at every parameter value. [Figure 12.6.1. Frequentist coverage of the 95\% credible interval for the air-flow coefficient against the true coefficient, for the prior of Chapter 7 and for a prior with slope standard deviations divided by five (4000 data sets per point). The flat-prior interval covers 0.95 everywhere.] Figure 12.6.1. Frequentist coverage of the 95\% credible interval for the air-flow coefficient against the true coefficient, for the prior of Chapter 7 and for a prior with slope standard deviations divided by five (4000 data sets per point). The flat-prior interval covers 0.95 everywhere. [Frequentist coverage of the 95\% credible interval for the air-flow coefficient against the true coefficient, for the prior of Chapter 7 and for a prior with slope standard deviations divided by five (4000 data sets per point). The flat-prior interval covers 0.95 everywhere.] Frequentist coverage of the 95\% credible interval for the air-flow coefficient against the true coefficient, for the prior of Chapter 7 and for a prior with slope standard deviations divided by five (4000 data sets per point). The flat-prior interval covers 0.95 everywhere. An informative prior makes intervals shorter, and better when the prior is sound; when it is not, they are confidently wrong. The frequentist interval makes no bet and pays in length. Chapter 27 meets the same trade-off as bias against variance. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Is the equal-tailed interval of @thm-ci-bayes-credible(d) the HPD interval for \sigma^2? Describe the HPD interval and explain the difference. No. The inverse gamma density is skewed to the right, so the HPD interval [l,u], with \pi(l\mid\y)=\pi(u\mid\y), is shifted toward smaller values. It also depends on the parameterization: the HPD interval for \log\sigma^2 does not transform into the one for \sigma^2, while equal-tailed intervals do. [A2] For u>2, find the posterior predictive mean and variance of a single future observation at \x_0. Why is the variance larger than au^2(1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0)? From @thm-ci-bayes-credible(c), Y_0\mid\y=\x_0\T\mathbf{m}_n+ au\sqrt{1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0}\,T with T\sim t( u), so the mean is \x_0\T\mathbf{m}_n and the variance is au^2(1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0)\, u/( u-2). The extra factor comes from the uncertainty about \sigma^2: given \sigma^2 the predictive variance is \sigma^2(1+\x_0\T\V_n\x_0), and averaging over the posterior gives \E(\sigma^2\mid\y)=b_n/(a_n-1), which exceeds au^2=b_n/a_n by the factor a_n/(a_n-1)= u/( u-2). B. Practice [B1] Under the g-prior of @prp-opt-shrinkage(c) with \mathbf{m}_0= zero, show that the credible interval for lambda\T beta is centred at \{g/(1+g)\} lambda\T\hbeta and has half-width t_{ u,\alpha/2}\, au\sqrt{g/(1+g)}\sqrt{ lambda\T(\X\T\X)^{-1} lambda}. Compare it with the t interval as g o\infty, paying attention to u and au^2. With \V_0=g(\X\T\X)^{-1}, \V_n=\{g/(1+g)\}(\X\T\X)^{-1} and \mathbf{m}_n=\{g/(1+g)\}\hbeta (@prp-opt-shrinkage(c)). Substitute in @thm-ci-bayes-credible(a). As g o\infty the centre and the matrix tend to those of least squares, but u=2a_0+n stays larger than n-p and au^2=b_n/a_n tends to (2b_0+ ext{SSE})/(2a_0+n), not to s^2. The interval does not become the t interval: that needs the flat prior on \sigma^2 as well, with a_0=-p/2 and b_0=0 (@cor-opt-flat-prior). [B2] Two future observations are taken at the same \x_0. Show that, under the posterior predictive distribution, they are correlated, and find the correlation. Why are they correlated when their errors are independent? Are they independent under the frequentist model? By @thm-ci-bayes-credible(c) with \X_0 having two equal rows \x_0\T, the scale matrix is au^2 igl(\I_2+h one one\T igr) with h=\x_0\T\V_n\x_0, so the correlation is h/(1+h). Both observations share the unknown beta (and \sigma^2), and uncertainty about the shared mean correlates them. Under the frequentist model with fixed parameters the two observations are independent, but the two prediction errors Y_{0j}-\hat{Y}_0 share \hat{Y}_0 and have the same correlation h_0/(1+h_0) under the flat prior. C. Going deeper [C1] Let \X have rank r

title: 12.7 Summary and Notes
content: Summary and Notes Summary 1. Confidence sets come from pivots, and are the sets of values that a family of level-\alpha tests accepts (@def-ci-confidence-set, @prp-ci-duality). 2. For estimable \blambda\T\bbeta, \blambda\T\hbeta\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{\blambda\T\G\blambda} is exact and free of the generalized inverse (@thm-ci-estimable-interval). A non-estimable function has no confidence set of finite expected length (@prp-ci-nonestimable). The interval for \sigma^2 is exact under normality and fragile without it (@prp-ci-sigma). 3. The confidence ellipsoid for \bLambda\T\bbeta is the acceptance region of the F test, shaped by the covariance of the estimates (@thm-ci-ellipsoid); all such ellipsoids are images of one ball around \hY (@prp-ci-mean-ball). Its shadows are Scheffé-type intervals (@lem-ci-cauchy-schwarz, @cor-ci-shadows). 4. The prediction interval \hat{Y}_0\pm t_{n-r,\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_0} never shrinks below the noise (@thm-ci-prediction-interval). The leverage h_0 is a Mahalanobis distance that reveals hidden extrapolation (@prp-ci-new-leverage). Without normality prediction intervals stay wrong as n\to\infty (@prp-ci-pi-limit). 5. The Working–Hotelling band, with multiplier \sqrt{kF_\alpha(k,n-r)}, covers the regression surface over a k-dimensional family exactly; k=2 for a straight line (@thm-ci-working-hotelling). 6. Fieller sets for ratios, and calibration sets, are exact, and are intervals, two rays or the whole line (@prp-ci-fieller, @thm-ci-calibration). The classical calibration estimator has no mean (@prp-ci-ratio-no-mean), and unbounded sets cannot be avoided (@prp-ci-calibration-unbounded). 7. Conjugate credible sets and predictive intervals have the frequentist shapes (@lem-ci-mvt, @thm-ci-bayes-credible) and equal them under the flat prior (@cor-ci-flat-agreement). Their coverage is nominal on average over the prior, not pointwise (@prp-ci-average-coverage). Notes and sources Confidence intervals and duality. Confidence intervals, and their construction by inverting tests, are due to Neyman (1937). Lehmann and Romano (2005) develop the duality and its optimality consequences. The two one-sided tests procedure of @exr-ci-equivalence is due to Schuirmann (1987). The shortest interval for a normal variance (@exr-ci-shortest-sigma) was worked out by Tate and Klett (1959). The source books. The chapter covers Seber and Lee (2003, chapter 5 and sections 6.1–6.5), Rencher and Schaalje (2008, sections 8.6–8.7) and Sen and Srivastava (1990, section 3.8). These books state the intervals for full-rank models; here they are stated for estimable functions in models of any rank, as in Christensen (2020). Rencher and Schaalje (2008, section 8.7) derive the F test as a likelihood ratio test, which Chapter 11 covers (@thm-glh-lrt). Hahn and Meeker (1991) is a practical guide to confidence, prediction and tolerance intervals. Bands. The band for a straight line is due to Working and Hotelling (1929), and the general projection argument to Scheffé (1953). Exact bands over finite intervals are due to Wynn and Bloomfield (1971) and constant-width bands to Gafarian (1964). Miller (1981) surveys the early literature and Liu (2010) gives a modern book-length treatment. Normality and prediction. The warning about conditional coverage after a preliminary test is from Olshen (1973). Ratios and calibration. Fieller’s method came from bioassay and is set out in general form in Fieller (1954). Krutchkoff (1967) proposed the inverse estimator and Hoadley (1970) gave its Bayesian interpretation. Osborne (1991) reviews calibration, and Brown (1993) treats the multivariate case. Gleser and Hwang (1987) proved the general form of @prp-ci-calibration-unbounded. Bayesian intervals. Box and Tiao (1973) and Gelman et al. (2013) treat credible and predictive intervals for the normal linear model under conjugate and flat priors. Data. The murder-rate data are the 2009 US state data of statsmodels; the stack loss data are from Brownlee (1965); the assay is simulated. References - Box, George E. P. and Tiao, George C. (1973). Bayesian Inference in Statistical Analysis. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley. - Brown, Philip J. (1993). Measurement, Regression, and Calibration. Oxford: Clarendon Press. - Brownlee, K. A. (1965). Statistical Theory and Methodology in Science and Engineering. 2nd edition. New York: Wiley. - Christensen, Ronald (2020). Plane Answers to Complex Questions: The Theory of Linear Models. 5th edition. Cham: Springer. - Fieller, E. C. (1954). Some Problems in Interval Estimation. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 16(2), 175–185. - Gafarian, A. V. (1964). Confidence Bands in Straight Line Regression. Journal of the American Statistical Association 59(305), 182–213. - Gelman, Andrew, Carlin, John B., Stern, Hal S., Dunson, David B., Vehtari, Aki and Rubin, Donald B. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis. 3rd edition. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press. - Gleser, Leon Jay and Hwang, Jiunn Tzon (1987). The Annals of Statistics 15(4), 1351–1362. - Hahn, Gerald J. and Meeker, William Q. (1991). Statistical Intervals: A Guide for Practitioners. New York: Wiley. - Hoadley, Bruce (1970). title: Multiplicity: Scheffé, Tukey, Bonferroni and the False Discovery Rate
content: Multiplicity: Scheffé, Tukey, Bonferroni and the False Discovery Rate A test with error rate 0.05 keeps that promise only when it is the only inference drawn from the data. A regression analysis rarely stops at one: it compares every pair of groups, examines each of many coefficients, and follows a significant F test with the contrast that looks most interesting. This chapter measures the error of a whole family of inferences and controls it in four ways. Scheffé’s method covers every estimable function in a subspace, even functions chosen after seeing the data, and is exactly the F test read one direction at a time. Tukey’s studentized range is exact for all pairwise differences of balanced means. Bonferroni’s inequality, and Holm’s sharper step-down version, need only the level of each test. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls the expected proportion of false discoveries, which is what screening many hypotheses needs. The chapter ends with a guide to choosing among them. What you need. The normal linear model and the sampling distributions of Chapter 7 (@thm-opt-sampling, @cor-opt-t, @cor-opt-quadratic), independence of projections from Chapter 4 (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections), and orthogonal projections onto subspaces from Chapter 6 (@thm-proj-nested, @thm-proj-constraint-space). Estimable functions and contrasts in the one-way layout come from Chapter 8 (@thm-est-oneway-contrasts, @prp-est-contrast-ss), and the sum of squares of a linear hypothesis from Chapter 9 (@thm-ss-hypothesis).
